subtopic: REPORT ON RETIREMENT AND SUPERANNUATION PRESENTED BY THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. WILLIAM ALVES BOYS (South Simcoe) presented the fourth report of the Special Committee appointed to consider the possibility of reducing or rearranging the staffs of the Inside Civil Service with a view to securing the greatest efficiency with the minimum number of employees, as follows:
Friday, June 7, 1919.
Your Committee having had before them the report of the Civil Service Commission made to the Governor in Council, pursuant to Order in Council dated 17th April, 1918, and having considered that portion thereof relating to the retirement and superannuation of certain officials therein referred to, and having heard evidence upon the question from a number of witnesses called and examined under oath, are of the opinion that such officials, owing to their age or permanent impairment of health, should be retired with a reasonable superannuation allowance, and with that end in view, your Committee beg to recommend that immediate
action be taken to give effect to the said report so far as the same relates to the officials therein referred to; and further that the necessary steps be taken to add to the list of such officials, for a like purpose, the names of any other employee in the Inside Civil Service, who for similar reasons might, with advantage to the service, be retired therefrom upon a like superannuation allowance.
All which is respectfully submitted. PROHIBITION.

Dear Mr. Rowell,
Referring to your letter of the 26th ultimo, with regard to the prohibition of inter-provincial trade in intoxicating liquor, and submitting the
41,34

question as to whether in view of section 121 of the British North America Act 1867 the Dominion has the power to prohibit this trade between provinces, I observe that section 121 applies only to articles of the growth, produce or manufacture of any one of the provinces, and as to such intoxicating liquor, as is of this description, I am of the opinion that this section does not limit the power of prohibition possessed by the Dominion, because the object of it is to declare immunity from taxation rather than, to affect the power which the Dominion otherwise has to prohibit exportation from one province to another of articles which parliament may consider ought not, for the peace, order and good government of Canada, to be admitted in the latter province. Section 121 occurs, as you will perceive, in a fascicle of clauses entitled revenues ; debts; assets; taxation; and is not directed as I eonoeive, against the prohibition of commodities, or trading inter-provineially or otherwise in commodities which in the general interest it may be deemed desirable to forbid.
While for these reasons I do not consider that there is any ground for substantial doubt of the power of the Dominion.to prohibit interprovincial trading such as above referred to I would suggest that the possibility of questioning the validity of the proposed legislation as to transportation of intoxicating liquors would be very much reduced, or in fact entirely disappear if in the proposed legislation the terms of the announcement of the 22nd December, 1917, were adhered to. That announcement did not refer to inter-provincial transportation of liquor in particular but simply declared that transportation of liquor into any part of Canada wherein the sale of intoxicating liquor is illegal will be prohibited on and after April 1st, 1918.
Dealing, with the matter in this way has the advantage of making clear that the purpose of the legislation is not to interfere in any way with inter-provincial trade as such, but to ensure the due observance of the legally enacted laws in all parts of the Dominion. The Canada Temperance Act contains an analogous prohibition as to the transportation of liquor into districts where that Act is in force and legislation in the terms I now suggest would be in effect merely extending that prohibition so as to cover the transportation into any area wherein the sale of liquor is by or under any law. Dominion or provincial, prohibited.
Dealing with the matter in this way would I think, make it clear that the legislation was by reason of its unmistakable purpose, clearly enacted in the exercise of the power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada and preclude any suggestion that it was intended to hamper in any way interprovincial trade as such.
In view of these consideration, I would advise the matter be dealt with in this manner.
Yours sincerely,
C. J. Doherty.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways):
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It will be remembered that forty-two or forty-three amendments were made to this Bill by the House as it came from the Senate, and when returned to the Senate four of those amendments were refused. A motion was made by the Prime Minister, that this House do agree to the consequen-

tial amendment made by the Senate to clause 262. There remain three clauses, and I would like to dispose of them to-day. Therefore I beg leave to move, Mr. Speaker:
That this House do insist upon the amendment made to section 32:5 of Bill No. 19, the amendment having been agreed to at the free conference between the two Houses.

I would like to oppose this motion.. Those who were present the other night when this matter came up will remember that I then made certain statements in regard to it. I explained that this clause was a very important, drastic, and far reaching one, and that the effect of it has not yet been fully considered by this House. It renders inoperative all statutes and agreements fixing rates, although the railway companies are allowed to retain charters, and other rights and privileges, obtained in consideration of those agreements. Now this affects a great many of the municipalities in Canada; it affects those in British Columbia, Ontario, Manitoba, and I think in otheT provinces. It also affects agreements which are entered into, for instance, by the province of Manitoba. It affects likewise the Crowsnest Pass agreemant. It has the effect of cancelling all the privileges which were obtained when the railway companies secured charters for their lands. Furthermore it has the effect of wiping out pending litigation, for instance, the Burnaby appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, which I discussed when this Bill was last before the House. It seems to me that is a most unusual and unprecedented proceeding. So far as I am aware it is usual in enactments of this kind to protect pending litigation, and I submit that some provision should have been made in this subsection to take care of at least pending litigation. I submit that interested parties have been allowed no opportunity to be heard. There has been no discussion in the press about this particular amendment, although it is of such great importance, and I think if this subsection is passed in its present form, when the public become acquainted with the effect and purport of it there will be a hue and cry raised all over Canada. Notwithstanding the fact British Columbia is very seriously affected by this amendment, the union of British Columbia municipalities knew nothing whatever about it until I wired them a few days ago. Although a great many municipalities in other parts of Canada were affected, the union of Canadian municipalities were not aware of this amendment. Both of these very important
organizations are now very strongly opposed to it. I have in my hand a letter which is written by the secretary of the union of Canadian municipalities written to the right hon. the Prime Minister, dated June 13, 1919, which is as follows:
The following is a copy of a telegram from the President of the Union of British Columbia Municipalities:
New Westminster, June 9, 1919. W. D. Lighthall, K.C.,
Hon. Secy. Union of Canadian Municipalities.
" Union of B. C. Municipalities asks cooperation of Union of Canadian Municipalities in opposing proposed amendment to Sec. 325 Railway Act toy which power will be given to Railway Commission to increase fares or rates notwithstanding provisions of any subsisting agreements between Railways and Municipalities, which is a direct violation of all the principles of contracts and agreements. Immediate action is necessary."
Fraser,
President.
To which we at once replied:
Wire received. We agree with you and will gladly co-operate.
W. I>. Lighthall,
Hon. Sec., U.C.M.
There was practically no discussion in the Special Committee in reference to this amendment. I have here a copy of the report of the proceedings of that committee dealing with this particular subsection, and possibly I might be permitted to read it:

That is the clause which I have already read. The report continues:

Chairman of the Railway Board?
Hon. Mr. Reid:	I would think so.
Mr. Mowat: Then he must have found cases where he needed it.
One of the cases where apparently it was needed was the particular case which is to go to the Supreme Court of Canada, the appeal which the Burnaby municipality has taken to the Supreme Court from the decision of the Board of Railway 'Commissioners.
The original application first came before the Board of Railway Commissioners at Ottawa in August of last year in the shape of an application by the British Columbia Electric Railway Company for approval oi an increased tariff of rates on a line belonging to that company, running between New Westminster and Vancouver. The reeve and other representatives of the municipality considered the matter so important that they came all the way from British Columbia to Ottawa to oppose that application. The hearing took all day, and aftei full discussion the decision of the board was reserved, as it was stated, for the purpose of awaiting the result of pending litigation. It seems that at the same time another appeal was threatened to the Supreme Court of Canada, but that appeal not having been proceeded with, in November of last year decision was given approving the rates and the holding that the board had jurisdiction to approve increased rates, notwith-
standing the existence of an agreement between Burnaby municipality and the British Columbia Electric Railway Company, fixing the maximum rates to be charged. The municipality immediately applied to the board for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada on the question of law involved, namely, whether the board had jurisdiction to grant that application or not. The board intimated that leave would be given on a definite question or on definite questions of law which would have to be settled by the board. Subsequently, in December of last year, the matter again came before the board at Ottawa, for the purpose of settling this question of law, and decision was reserved for a subsequent hearing at Vancouver, which hearing took place in February of this year. In February, the matter was again discussed at length and as to the particular question of definite law to be submitted, and it was promised that a decision should be handed down very shortly. A decision has never been given, and the question of law has never been settled, although many applications have been made to the chairman of the board to have the matter disposed of.
This amendment was apparently drawn by the chairman of the board, either at his suggestion or at the suggestion of the minister; but at whose suggestion I am, of course, not able to determine from the reports of the committee, because at one place it is stated that it was at the chairman's suggestion and at another place that it was drawn by the chairman at the suggestion of the minister. The point that strikes me as peculiar is this: Why is it necessary for the Minister of Railways to go to the Board of Railway Commissioners to draw up an amendment of this kind? Surely there are in the department proper and capable officers who can draw up the necessary legislation. The situation as I see it is this. If the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners considers it necessary to increase rates throughout Canada, what chance have the public on an application coming before the board dealing with a matter of this kind? The principle is wrong, and a tribunal of this character appointed for the purpose of dealing with applications of this nature should not, beforehand, be brought into the matter at all. Personally I have the very highest respect for the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and for the other members of the board, and I do not think they would do anything but give the fairest of hearing on any application which came before them. At the same

time, I think, in a case like 'this, the board might very well 'be left out of it. Anothei point that appears to me to be wrong in principle is this. The fact that the Government is forced, against its will, into the transportation business, is no reason why it should endeavour to make the public using other railroads pay increased rates, because that is what the matter comes to. If the Government is compelled to increase the rates to such an extent as will make the railway pay, what chance have the public? This clause 325 should not be passed at this time. If the minister has a good case-and perhaps he has-he should not be afraid to discuss it in this House and let the public know about it. Let there be a full discussion about the matter in this House, and, if after a full discussion, this House decides the amendment should be passed in its present form, then I think the public will be satisfied. (Interested parties should have the privilege of stating their objections to this amendment, a privilege -which they have not yet had. I would suggest to the minister that he drop this clause at the present time, and if he cares to do so, that he should bring forward another Bill dealing with this particular matter, and when that Bill comes before the House it can be fully discussed and we shall know what we are doing.
Mr. ROBERT LORNE RICHARDSON
(Springfield): I would like to say just a word on this point, but first I should like to as!k a question of the minister. Was the Manitoba Government consulted before this clause was suggested by the Chairman of the Railway Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Manitoba Government was aware that this motion was up. I did not consult with that Government myself.

The reason I asked the question is this. If this clause passes, it seems to me that it interferes in a very improper manner with an arrangement the Manitoba Government made years ago. When Mackenzie and Mann were building their system in the West, the Manitoba Government aided their road. I am not quite sure as to what portion of the road received aid, but I think it was that portion between Winnipeg and Port Arthur that was granted very substantial aid, and as a condition of that aid the Manitoba Government secured a certain rate on wheat. That was to be a gratuity. If this clause passes, that rate is vitiated, is disposed of altogether, and the rates on that
road may be increased away beyond the point which the Manitoba Government arranged for, and the people of Manitoba have a very substantial claim on the Federal Government for depriving them of an advantage which they secured and which they paid for in a very substantial manner. If provision were made that Manitoba was to be reimbursed for the amount of the subsidy she granted to the Canadian Northern people in days gone by, no complaints might be raised, but a substantial injustice will be done to the province of Manitoba if this clause is adopted. I would say, as a representative of a Manitoba constituency, that the Manitoba Government ought to be cited to appear here because the interests of that province are going to be highly prejudiced should this clause pass. It may be, as the minister pointed out, that increased rates are necessary because of the increased wages that are to be paid. [DOT] I have nothing to say as to that, but Manitoba, I repeat, secured certain rate advantages by the payment of a substantial subsidy, and I think this House ought to pause before depriving Manitoba in this perfunctory manner, and without the knowledge of the Provincial Government, of those advantages.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I suggest that as long as the whole matter is a railway question, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr Peck) or the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), or any other hon. gentleman who wishes to express views on clause 325 may be permitted to say what they have

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think, in view of the peouliar, and perhaps I may add unfortunate, circumstances, the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition is a very excellent one, and so far as the -Chair is concerned,
I shall be only too glad to give any hon. gentleman full latitude to discuss the merits of that clause.

I wish to say very little on the clause, but I wanted to see a vote taken because it is well to have the municipalities know which iway the members vote on a question of this kind. If this clause passes, the Board of Railway Commissioners will have the right to abrogate any bargain in regard to rates which the municipality may have made. I think there is a tendency in this House to override the municipalities and infringe upon their rights, and some hon. gentlemen will have the fact.brought to their attention in the next election. If this clause carries I cannot see how any municipality can ever again enter into a bargain with the railroad with regard to rates. The railways hare come from time immemorial to the provincial government and even to the Dominion Government asking for concessions, and the only way in which they can be bargained with, from a municipal point of view, if the franchise is granted, is to get a guarantee in regard to rates. But if this passes, the guarantee will be no good, because the railroads will put up a howl that they are losing money, and the bargain in regard to rates will be overridden, so far as the municipalities are concerned.

This is a very serious proposition now before Parliament, namely, the over-riding of all previous legislation in the matter in question, whereby the municipalities and provinces were given special privileges in regard to railway rates by certain companies. I know of instances where municipalities secured special privileges or rights .which were crystallized in Acts of the Legislature and of Parliament and were of great value to them. Now they are to be wiped out without the municipalities being heard. Not only the municipalities but the provinces and the general public have been guaranteed certain rights in regard to rates, which will be abolished or at any rate will be subject to modification by' the Railway Board. While I am in favour of the Railway Board having wide powers, at the same time, when great changes of this kind are
proposed I think those interested should have full opportunity of discussing them in this House, and I would suggest that this special clause go over until next session when those interested, namely, the farmers of the West, could be heard. These farmers of the West have .important Tights guaranteed them by agreements confirmed by legislation; so have the people of Ontario; and the people of all Canada have similar rights in connection with the Crows-nest Pass, in which the Pacific railway is interested. I see no reason why this special clause should not stand over until next session when every one can be heard. I know that the Board of Railway Commissioners are confronted with the question of increasing rates -and these special clauses as they now exist have the effect of injuring in a degree the general public. Inasmuch as they have these rights which have been crystallized in Acts of Parliament, an opportunity should be given for these several parties to be heard. Another matter calls for public protest. In the Act passed last session Parliament placed all the Government railways of the country under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Heretofore Parliament and the Department of Railways were free to do anything they saw fit an connection with rates or anything else connected with the Government railways, which we now call the National railways. Parliament has divested itself of any rights it had in regard to rates on Government railways, the Intercolonial included, and has put the power in the hands of the Railway Commission. Now it is proposed also to place in the hands of the commissioners the revision of the rates that were conceded to some western provinces and the rates conceded the municipalities. I happen to know of a little municipality that had certain rates guaranteed it by Act of the Legislature of Ontario. Then the jurisdiction of that railway passed from the Legislature of Ontario to the Dominion Parliament anid the municipality appealed to the Dominion Government for relief which it did not quite get. I do not think that any single municipality should be deprived of its rights in an agreement ratified by the legislature and by this House, and inasmuch as these are far-reaching considerations and the people and farmers of the West have certain rights guaranteed them in regard to their products, especially in connection with the movement of wheat, under that agreement made with the province of Ontario, I think the Government



*would not only be wise, but extremely fair, if they decided that an Act of such great importance should be left over for another session, especially in view of the fact that probably we are to have another session this year. While I do not deny the necessity that appears to he imposed upon the Railway Commissioners to help the railways to meet their obligations by a revision of the rates, I think that the question of revision should not be made operative until these various parties-the general public, the people of the provinces, and of the municipalities who have these guaranteed rates-have an ample opportunity of presenting their case to Parliament.

It is only fair that I should give my reason for taking the stand I have taken on this question. We have a radial railway running from Hamilton to Burlington and Oakville owned by the Cataract Power Company, who entered into an agreement with the town of Burlington to carry passengers at a certain fare. A by-law was passed by the town of Burlington and ratified by the Ontario Government and is in existence up to the present time. This Act now before us is calculated to give the power to the Railway Board to fix the rate for passengers which has been already fixed under the by-law. the railway company, in operating on that road, were charging 20 cents from Sherman avenue to Burlington and 25 cents from the radial station to Burlington, some 23 miles, or a little over a cent a mile. The town of Burlington refused to allow the Railway Board to fix the rate.
The outcome was that the railway company took off their cars, quit running the road for six weeks and left the people of that section without railway facilities. There was no way in or out between Hamilton and Burlington. Burlington Beach is a summer resort, between 800 and 1,000 people live there, a great many people go in and out every day and at the time the railway company took off their cars the Railway Board had no power to interfere because of this by-law. It went along for some time until the town of Burlington had a meeting and passed a resolution asking the Dominion Government to enact such legislation as would place the railway company under the control of the Railway Board. The mayor of Burlington came down, appeared before the special committee, read the resolution, and showed that it was the wish of the town of Burlington that the by-law be set aside and power vested in the Railway Board. This was agreed to and the Bill

went through. Then, the Bill went to the Senate and you know what happened there.
What I have said to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. iMcQuarrie) is that I have no intention whatever, in trying to get this amendment through, of interfering with any other municipality. I have no objection to the Act being so amended as to provide that a municipality which grants a bonus to, or enters into an agreement with, any railway company in regard to fares and other matters shall not be interfered with The provision which I ask for is not intended to apply to a municipality which has granted a bonus or entered into an arrangement of that kind. In our case the municipality has given no bonus. The people of Burlington are desirous that this amendment shall go through and that the right shall be given to the Railway Board to say what the fares shall be hereafter. I do not know of any reason why their wish in that regard should not be granted. This is not going to take any rights away from any municipality. We have no objection to the Bill being amended in any way so long as it concedes the desire of a municipality which has not granted a bonus to a railway company to have the matter placed under the Railway Board. I do not see any good reason why that should not be allowed. That is what I wanted in the first place when I tried to get this clause framed in a different way. I was told by Sir Henry Drayton and others that it would not be possible to do this. The Act would have to be a general Act that would apply to every section of the country. I did not get my way in that regard; hence, the clause went through in the way it is. It would be most unfair to the people of Hamilton and Burlington if this amendment were thrown out this session and the railway company were allowed to repeat what they have already done. That is what I want to prevent. I want it placed in such a position that the railway company cannot stop running their cars without reference to the Board of Railway Commissioners. There is no reason why the Act should not give the Board of Railway Commissioners the right to protect the people of these municipalities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I rather regret a practice that now seems to be gaining strength and recognition in this country of trying to settle lawsuits by Ac't of Parliament. I think it is a practice that is likely to get the House and the Government into a good deal of trouble. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) has just stated a case

which appears to be a specific difficulty between the city of Hamilton and some railway company concerning a contract that they entered into. That difficulty should be settled in the Supreme* Court of Ontario if there is a misunderstanding about their contract. If there was tno power even in the Supreme Court to enforce that contract it might ultimately be necessary to come to this Parliament. But I submit it is a bad habit to be passing general Acts of Parliament with a view to meeting, or dealing with, one specific case. That is what I have to say about legislation of this character. I think it is unusual, and I would be almost disposed to say improper, for a judge of the Supreme Court of any of our provinces, who had delivered a decision on a certain matter and while that decision was open to appeal, and possibly an appeal pending, to come to this Parliament and ask, suggest, or draft, an Act of Parliament to be put through which would have a material effect upon his own decision. I would regard that on the part of a judge of the Supreme Court as something highly improper. I think the Chairman of the Railway Board is just as important as any single judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, if not more so. I would regard it as irregular for the chairman of the board, while his own decision and that of the board was pending, or standing for appeal, to come to this Parliament and suggest, much less to allow himself to draft, a section to be passed through this House which materially affected his own decision or the decision of the board. That ds the way I understand the explanation of hon. gentlemen supporting the Government.
I have no personal knowledge of the matter that in this case comes before this Parliament, but I would say that a decision ' given by any tribunal must stand or fall upon the facts and the law at the time that decision is given and it should not be affected by legislation that was passed afterwards. The decision must stand or fall upon that and if Parliament finds it necessary to step in afterwards and pass remedial legislation to remedy an evil, that is another matter. That ds very often done. The decision must take its count and must stand or fall upon the law and the facts as they existed at the time of the hearing.
Coming down to the particular matter that was dealt with by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) and the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) with regard to these contracts with
the provinces of British Columbia and Manitoba and other contracts that are outstanding, I submit to the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) that nothing should happen in this House, nothing should be countenanced in this House by way of legislation, that would affect these contracts until the fullest possible or necessary hear-* ing has>
been given to all parties concerned. The province of Manitoba and the province of British Columbia entered into these contracts-
And the whole people of Canada in connection with the Crowsnest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was dealing with these contracts entered into in good faith, for the advantage of those provinces no doubt, giving subsidies to these companies with the view that fair and reasonable rates would always be maintained in those provinces by virtue of this arrangement. I submit to the Government and to this House that it is far from fair and equitable dealing to change these conditions by an Act of this Parliament without giving these people an opportunity of being heard. I am sure the Prime Minister, if he understood this question, would be very loath to agree to contracts that had been solemnly entered into between companies and Governments in this country being overridden and rendered useless without giving the parties, who have given consideration to them and who have paid out their money and the money of their governments, an opportunity to be heard in support of these agreements. All that is to be set aside and rendered as if it had never existed by this Parliament which has really had nothing to do with the initiating of these contracts.
I submit that these things should not happen. The same thing applies to the contract entered into some years ago between this Government and the Canadian Pacific.
I understand, although I was not in the House at that time, that it was in 1902 or 1903 that the arrangement was made-
That was the year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am pretty sure, Mr. Speaker, that it was before dny becoming a member of Parliament in 1904, for I do not remember this agreement being discussed, although I have often heard it referred to. But, at all events, it does not

make any difference. That agreement broke up what was regarded as a monopoly, and while it has been of advantage to the Canadian Pacific railway, it has also been

of advantage to the Canadian people. Now, that that agreement should not be any longer regarded by the Canadian Pacific rail-, way or by this Government without its being fully discussed in this House and an opportunity given to all parties concerned to be heard, is, I think, a line of practice that should not be encouraged. That agreement is of far-reaching importance to the people of Canada, and, Sir, it should not be set aside in this- summary fashion. Full notice should have been given that the effect of this amendment to the general Railway Act was to strike at agreements of this character. Speaking for myself, I had not the slightest idea from what I heard discussed in connection with section 325 that it had anything to do with the agreement between the Government of Manitoba and some railway company, or with the agreement between the Government of British Columbia and municipalities in that province and some railway company, or that it affected the Crowsnest Pass agreement. With all due respect to my good friend the Minister of Railways, who is responsible for this amendment, I think its purport should have been fully explained to the House. If anything can be done now to give the parties interested an opportunity of being heard,
I am sure the Government ought to take the necessary steps to that end. If the province of Manitoba or of British Columbia gave a subsidy to a road, with the understanding that only rates approved by the province were to be charged, and we step in as a Government and take over that road and break the agreement, there is nothing clearer to my mind than that we should pay back any subsidy so paid. We cannot hold the money and at the same time take away the benefits which the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia were to obtain from the bargains they made.
I am sorry, -Sir, that we are passing general Acts when we should be dealing with specific cases. If it is necessary to legislate in order to settle the difficulty between the city of Hamilton and the railway company referred -to, and if this is the only place where that can be settled, let us deal with it by a specific Act entirely upon its merits, -and not by a general Act which may suit one case and affect a thousand other cases where the parties have no opportunity to be heard.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the House to one or two considerations that perhaps have not been taken entirely into account. In view of the enor-

mous increase in the cost of operation due to the increased cost of material and labour, we found it absolutely necessary to pass the Order in Council which has been laid upon the table of*the House, enabling rates to be raised, notwithstanding the existence of agreements such as have been mentioned here this morning. We had our choice between the bankruptcy and cessation of operation of the railways and taking that step. There was absolutely no alternative. It was a difficult alternative, and we were obliged to act according to our idea of what was best in the public interest. This clause, which is being discussed under the direction of the hon. the Speaker, is to continue that right after the Order in Council shall have ceased to operate.
I have had the advantage of reading a very carefully prepared memorandum from the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, in which he makes it abundantly plain-to me, at least-that for .the future the board must have the right which is to be established by that clause, otherwise it would be absolutely impossible for it to fix rates commensurate with the necessity of having the railways operated. If a score or' fifty or one hundred agreements are made all over Canada between municipalities or provinces and railway companies, by which the fixing of uniform rates for all railway companies-an absolute necessity where many lines are competing-is entirely prevented, well, the Board of Railway Commissioners, so far as the fixing of rates is concerned, -might as well be abolished. It cannot function properly, because it cannot establish a uniform- system of rates throughout Canada if it is to be restricted here as to one company and there as to another company and somewhere else as to another company in respect to rates. Therefore, I say that so far as the future is concerned it seems to me that this clause is an absolute necessity.
So far as the past is concerned, there are other considerations which certainly do arise, and I have felt the force of them during the discussion which has been going on for the last hour. I should ire quite content, if we had not passed the clause, to have it so amended that it should continue in force for -a period of, say, three years only, during which time we would have an opportunity of considering the whole situation from any standpoint-from the standpoint of limitations, if any, upon the effect of this clause in the future; from the standpoint of compensation, possibly, by a railway company which had agreed to

carry traffic at a fixed rate and had received a certain 'advantage by (reason of that, and which was now at liberty to apply to the Railway Commission, under a clause such as this, for the purpose of having that agreement entirely set aside. I think there is some force in that proposal, and it seems to me we should consider it. I should not be at all disappointed if the (Senate in considering the amendment should reach the conclusion that the effect of this clause might very well be limited to a period of, say, three years, or two years, or something like that, during which period the considerations which have been pressed upon the attention of the Government this morning would be taken into account and a just result in the public interest would he arrived at. I hope that hon. members will accept my assurance that the Government is disposed to look after the question in that way. On the other hand, there is absolute necessity, if the Board of Railway Commissioners is to effectively discharge its functions, that it shall in future have the right , to deal with rates, irrespective of agreements of this character made in different parts of the country.

There is a great deal of force in the remarks of the Prime Minister that there should be some latitude in the application of rates during the war period, and I would have no objection to the passing of this clause, none whatever, were I fully satisfied that the Railway Commission would act fairly and equitably towards all parties concerned. But I must say that certain things that came under my notice recently with reference to decisions of the Railway Commission, which have led me to believe that that body, in the matter of freight rates, are acting entirely in the interests of the railway companies, and that they are putting into force decisions of a most reactionary character and which bear very heavily upon the poor people of this country and operate unjustly towards them. I refer principally to the western part of Ontario and to the freight rates on coal. The farmers need to have coal, and poor people require that commodity also, and you would have thought, Sir, that in their decisions in the matter oi freight rates on coal the Railway Commission would take great care and act judicially and equitably towards all parties concerned. A recent decision of the Railway Commission, however, operates in this way: Most of the coal that comes into Western Ontario from the United States has to pass through the yards in Buffalo, and an inter-switching
charge is enforced there of $8 a car. The question of absorbing that charge came up and the Railway Commission made a decision thereon. They decided that where there is competition between railways-for instance in the cities of Toronto and Hamilton-the railways shall absorb that charge* but where there is no competition-for example in the town of Port Credit where there is only one railway-the man who buys that coal must pay the inter-switching charge of $8 a car, which amounts to about twenty-five cents a ton in the case of every purchaser of coal at that place. On the other hand, in the city of Toronto, only a few miles farther on, where there is competition in railway rates, the railways have to absorb the charge of $8 per car and the people of that city are freed from any liability in connection with it. I would be quite willing to give the fixing of the rates all over this country at any time to a commission that would act fairly and equitable in the interests of the public generally. That is the intention of this country and of this Parliament. Our desire is to get away from the idea of railway competition so that people throughout the whole country -regardless of where they are living-will receive a fair deal no matterAvhether there is railway competition or not. In view of this fact I think the Government should seriously consider the handing over of this important matter when it involves the possibility of the perpetration of many acts of injustice towards the provinces and the municipalities without their being heard, solely in the interest of a particular company, or a particular corporation, in the city of Hamilton. I do not think this Parliament is supposed to legislate solely in the interests of the town of Burlington, the city of Hamilton, ot Sir John Gibson, much as I respect that gentleman. There are other questions to be considered, and if the Railway Commission are going to do their duty, as they should do, they will deal equitably towards all parties affected.
During the last year or two, since tire decision to increase railway rates all over the country was arrived at, it is impossible for anybody to inform themselves as to the Tailway rates in force and ascertain whether the mass of people, and communities in general, are being equitably dealt with by the railway companies. There is no schedule of the railway rates charged published in, the Canada Gazette from time to time, so that a person who has to ipay railway rates could find out what his neighbours or competitors are paying, or what

rates are in effect all over the country. The Government should seriously consider the effect of this clause at the present time. If I had not known of the circumstances in connection with the unjust coal rate to which I have referred, I would have been totally unaware that the poor man in every town and village-and this applies especially to communities in Western Ontario where the Grand Trunk is the sole railway-where there is no railway competition is called upon to pay this unjust charge of 25 cents a ton on coal, which the railways themselves should assume. Why should the people in those places be discriminated against in favour of the people living in cities simply because in the one case there is no railroad competition, and in the other case there is? That is no kind of treatment for a tribunal such as the Railway Commission to mete out to people, and therefore for the reasons which I have mentioned I very much dread the Railway Commission being given any such power as is now proposed to be conferred upon them.

I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. T. J. Stewart) withdraws his objection to a reconsideration of the previous resolution. In that case, I presume we might have the unanimous consent of the House to a reconsideration of clause 325 so that some amendment of it, such as has been suggested, might be made.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would point out that
there is a motion before the House that has not been disposed of, and which should be dealt with before passing to a reconsideration of a resolution previously entertained and adopted. The motion is in respect to clause 374. I am directing the attention of hon. gentlemen particularly to the circumstances because, under the Rules, hon. gentlemen are confined to one speech. If it is their desire to discuss clause 325 they should also hear in mind that the motion now before the House deals with section 374.

I deem it somewhat unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill should conflict in so many respects with the apparent rights of municipalities. If this were the only case we might not possibly attach so much importance to it, but such is not the case. The considerations which the right hon. the Prime Minister has just given us as to the special circumstances under which our railways are at present operating, of course, have naturally great weight. I am fully aware of the fact that

the railways cannot operate under the old rates and make ends meet at all. I think everybody must be thoroughly convinced that owing to the high price of all kinds of raw materials that enter into the construction of railways, and owing to the conditions of the labour market, and other facts, it is absolutely impossible for railways to operate, and do that successfully, under the rates that were in force a few years ago. But even after giving all due weight to those considerations it does appear to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. McQuarrie) has somewhat of a grievance in regard to clause 325 that has not been quite fairly met. I do not wish to reflect in any way upon your judgment, Mr. Speaker, in the matter, which I think was absolutely fair, but it was the intention, I think, of the hon. gentleman to submit an amendment to that particular clause and by its sudden adoption he was more or less debarred from moving the amendment which he probably otherwise would have done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must submit to the hon. gentleman that the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) spoke and resumed his seat, without moving any motion.	.

That is quite correct, Mr. Speaker, but I think it was his intention either to move an amendment himseli, or have some other hon. member do it for him. I dc nol desire to reflect in any way, Mr. Speaker, on the judgment you have delivered. I think it is perfectly fair, but it is unfortunate, so far as the Minister of Railways is concerned, that he did not reply in a convincing manner to the objections that were raised by the hon. gentleman. I think myself they were of sufficient importance t-o have called for a few words of explanation, and without desiring to at all cast any reflections upon the minister in respect to any wish to hurry legislation, I think the hon. gentleman's remarks should have been replied to in a way that would have been satisfactory to him. There are a great many municipalities in Canada concerned in this question, there is no doubt about that. Very many agreements have been entered into between municipalities and railways dating back for a long period, dealing with rates and with the running and stopping of trains, and many other matters, in which the whole agreement may be involved, and at this stage it does not appear to me that we quite know what agreements are going to be upset by a general standardization such as this particular kind of legislation in-

volves. I am just as anxious as the Minister of Railways to see this legislation go through, but when it )is passed I want, if possible, to 'have justice done to the municipalities all over Canada.
I do not think any good end will be gained by tearing up .agreements which have been in. existence for, many years and which have been lived up to by both parties for a long time. I should deplore it if, in the rushing of this clause or any other clause .through, the interests of municipalities-because I deem them supreme in certain limited and specified areas over which they exercise jurisdiction, or eminent domain, as, I think, the hon. member for Pafkdale (Mr. Mowat) would say-are in any way sacrificed. I trust, if we proceed to allow these clauses to go through, we shall see that in some way or another the interests of municipalities are not ruthlessly sacrificed and long standing agreements torn up by an Act of Parliament which, perhaps, the Chairman of the Railway Corflmission, I think the leader of the Opposition. (Mr. McKenzie) said, has a good deal to do with placing on the statute-books. While I do not object to that, I do not think it is a very wise precedent to establish. I say these few words only wHh a view to having it understood that, if we support the measure, we are still very strongly of .the opinion that municipal or provincial government contracts, which have also been drawn to our attention, should be carefully safeguarded so that no injustice may be done to those interested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Might I ask the indulgence of the House for the purpose of endeavouring to arrive at a conclusion which .will be satisfactory? After we have disposed of section 374, with which, technically at least, we are dealing at present, I purpose asking for the unanimous consent of the House to revert to the motion of the Minister of Railways with regard to section 325 in order to modify that motion, entirely with his consent, in the following manner:
That this House doth insist upon the amendment made to section 326 of Bill No. 19, hut with the following limiting provision thereto at the end thereof, that is to say,
" Provided that this subsection shall remain in force only during a period of three years from and after the date of the passing of this Act."
That will give us time in the interval to look into the question and to consider all these matters, and to determine whether or not some compensation Should not be
offered by railway companies or by those who represent them for concessions which have been made in consideration, of rates.

Might I ask the Prime Minister if he will add to that?
Pending litigation not to be affected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think, as regards that, I should rather like my hon. friend to accept the determination of the Railway Commission in the meantime. The Railway Commission is not bound to disregard; it is only authorized to disregard; but I think in the meantime, during the period of three years, as during the past eighteen months, we might leave those matters to 'be determined by the best judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that he either shorten that time or say that this Act shall not be operative for at least twelve or twenty-four months. That would give every one an opportunity to be heard in connection with the rights that are being taken away by the legislation as it was introduced into the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps we could proceed to discuss clause 374 now, and afterwards I shall ask for the unanimous consent of the House for the purpose of moving this motion, and I hope I may receive that consent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?
What is the question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has already discussed it.
Mr. Speaker

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has already spoken.

I do not find myself in agreement with the proposed motion of the minister, and I will briefly give my reasons. Since the discussion of this Bill in committee, which discussion took a long time, the public attention of the country has been fastened on the Bill with the result that an enormous volume of opinion opposed to the present position in which we find ourselves by reason of the refusal of the Senate to accept our amendment, has been heard. It seems to me that before we come to a decision now in pursuance of the motion of the minister, we should discuss the mat-

ter again with some new light that has been thrown upon it. The effect of the motion of the minister is to cut the Bill into two parts. I was not in the House when he was explaining his motion, but I understand his idea is to get rid of this clause in order that the general Railway Bill may go through. While it is highly desirable that the Railway Bill, minus this clause, should go through, it seems to me that the Government, in taking this course, is not dealing w'ith the matter in as proper a manner as it should. It is true you get rid of a troublesome clause, but by you doing so, the municipalities who are interested are thrown entirely on their own resources. It is just as if a parent were to deal with a troublesome or ailing child', not with comfort or kindness, but by ducking its head under water for the purpose of getting rid of it in order that the family life should go on. If this motion carries, the troublesome clause will be out; the general Railway Bill will sail through; the Government, who seem to be chiefly interested in- the Bill and not in the interest of the power clause and that of the municipalities will be perfectly satisfied, and this little Bill which the minister purposes bringing in for the regulation of electric power companies will be left by itself. We all know what is going to happen to that little Bill. The little Bill, if passed here in the way we decided upon the other day, namely, that the rights ol municipalities will be protected, will have just as much chance as a kitten would in a kennel of terriers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The remark of
the hon. gentleman was not in conformity with the rules.
Of course, I will withdraw the expression; I got into a colloquial frame of mind and used a colloquialism.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member was reflecting upon the proceedings of another Chamber.

Quite so. I was too colloquial. What I should like to see the Government do is this: To recognize more than it does the great feeling among the people of this country living in municipalities that they should receive more protection. Before the clause goes any further I should like to draw attention to one very important piece of law, namely, that owing to the stern brave fight put up by the municipalities beginning twenty years ago the law was so crystallized that a power company before it could put its trunk lines through a municipality had to obtain the munici-

pality's consent; if the consent of the municipality was withheld or refused, the company could go to the Railway Committee for the purpose of getting an order. But very different is the law with regard to selling or distributing electricity in municipalties. This Parliament has declared, and the law has been in force for years now, that the municipality is the sole judge as to whether a power company shall come in and sell electricity. The law in that respect is in this very section 247, which is referred to in the notice of motion of the minister. That being so, and although the municipalities have an absolute right to decline, if they so wish, to allow a selling company to come in or to erect poles or make condulets, yet the Senate has added this subclause 5 to the Bill which allows one particular company- because that is the way it works out-to go into any municipality in Canada.
At one o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock.

The present Railway Act, section 247, subsection 8 reads:
Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to authorize the company to exercise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages, without the company having first obtained consent therefor by a by-law of the municipality.
The effect of the rejection of our amendment by the Senate is that a particular company, though not mentioned, can come in without consent, therefore taking it out of the ordinary law. I cannot and I will not here take up any further time in repeating the arguments, legal or otherwise, which were advanced on the former occasion. If the new Bill suggested eventually comes before the House that contest will have to take place again. I have an amendment which I will read in a moment. This is a contest between a powerful aggregation of companies, interlocked in one way or another for their own purposes in financing, and the municipalities in Canada. It has been suggested, and I find that the advocates of the company never miss an opportunity to assert, that this is a Toronto Bill, in order that the people may take no interest in it believing it to be entirely local. But I was first interested in this movement by my sympathy with the association of municipalities and I cannot do better, to show the attitude of those municipalities, than by giving a short quotation from- the Canadian Municipal Journal published in Montreal for June. In discussing the debate and the proceed-

ings of this House earlier in this month it makes use of this language:
As a matter of fact if it had not been for the clauses in the present Railway Act protecting the municipalities from the action of corporate interests, and which were inserted after many a hard and bitter fight, municipal Canada would to-day be at the mercy of the goodwill of every franchise grabber who knew the art of lobbying at Ottawa. "What is more, we do not know of a single public utility owned by private interests, but what has at some time during its existence tried, even with the above protective clauses inserted in its charter, to beat the local authorities in some way or other.
That is the trouble and the disadvantage with which these, municipalities have to contend, and I may say that I have always been in sympathy with them in their struggles and was glad when they succeeded in inducing this Parliament to pass legislation which gave protection to municipalities. Therefore, I would not like to see that protection taken away except for the very strongest reasons. I am well aware that it is said a very strong reason exists because the company, by reason of a fortunate decision which they obtained from the Privy Council, acquired some rights. It is not necessary at this moment to deal with that question, except to say that I do not believe that any right has been invaded. We cannot question the decision of the Privy Council so far as it goes, but for those who were not in the House on the occasion of the last debate, I have simply to repeat that without doubt that decision in no way goes to the merits of the case. The law lords distinctly disclaimed any decision upon the policy as between the two interests, but simply gave a grammatical or technical interpretation of the Act. The Railway Act was consolidated in 1903, one year after the charter was granted; but the draftsman probably did not know that the Railway Act was incorporated in the charter and did not so draw the Acts that the protection was continued. Consequently, this company has slipped through the meshes of the law. But it is our law; 'we made the law. That was the understanding at the time, and Parliament has the right to go back now and declare the law to be what it intended it to be at that time. This is a fight not by the particular company in the charter and which is inferentially mentioned in the Senate amendment. It is a fight on the part of the Toronto Railway Company, because I hold in my hand a trust mortgage dated in 1911, by which the Toronto Power Company made an issue of bonds. Clause 65 in that mortgage reads: The Railway Company-
That is, the Toronto Railway Company-
-hereby absolutely and unconditionally guarantees the due payment by the company of principal and interest on stock and bonds for the time being, and also sinking fund payments for the redemption of bonds hereinbefore agreed to be made.
That is dated July 27, 1911. While it is difficult for us to follow the interlockings and different agreements between all these companies, yet the fact stands out clearly that we in 1902, in giving this charter to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, authorized them to make a bond issue of $1,500,000. They did make that issue and it all went to one company-one of the interlocking companies, the Electrical Development Company. So that that issue of bonds was not- bought by the public, who were in no wise interested in it. It was transferred to one of the interlocking companies. Now, Parliament had an object and a reason in limiting the bonds to $1,500,000, and when this company, chartered by us, enters into relations with other companies and says: "We have a bond issue of $30,000,000 now upon the whole," that is transgressing the power given by us in 1902 which limited the issue to the sum I have mentioned. Therefore, I say that vested rights are not affected and should not be held to be affected. No one in Canada wishes to interfere with vested rights, but there is something else besides finance, and that is, the right of municipalities to be sovereign in their own jurisdiction. We had petitions in the committee from 107 sources, and I believe there are a considerable number of others. The association of municipalities is represented from Alberta to Nova Scotia. This company has the right to go all over Canada, and its extremely valuable charter which we inadvertently gave is enhanced by this technical decision of the Privy Council. If we allow it to go through and do not reassert the position we took the other day we will give them the same power to interfere with the rights of any municipalities, which will be keenly resented and fought to the end. I therefore desire that we should re-assert the position we took two weeks ago and if it is proper that we should deal with the two clauses in the one motion, I may say that my hon. friend the member for West York (Mr. Wallace) who moved an amendment regarding clause 376, joins with me in this motion, which is as follows:
That all the words after the word " that " in the sixth line of the resolution be struck out and the following inserted in lieu thereof:
This House doth insist upon the amendment of clause 374 regarding: electrical power distri-

button in municipalities and clause 376 regarding increased compensation to be paid by rural telephone companies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This amendment is more or less technical and is before me for the first time, and there is some question as to whether it can be properly considered as an amendment to the motion before the House. However, I will put the amendment and reserve the right to give a decision on the point in a moment.
The resolution is that a certain message be sent to the Senate, and the effect of my amendment, if carried, would be to send a message other than that proposed.

I would like, now that I am in order, to refer to the question of the invasion of municipal rights in Ontario. The previous speaker referred to municipal rights as vested rights. If there are any vested rights that ought to be considered sacred in this country, I agree with him that the right of the municipalities to administer and control their own affairs ought to be so considered. Apparently that was the object of Sir James Whitney when he was Premier of Ontario. He introduced legislation to ensure that municipal rights would be protected. They had been raided before this from Ottawa by a party which had declared itself to be the champion of provincial and municipal rights. These municipal rights were invaded by transferring to the jurisdiction of the Dominion Parliament many companies that had been authorized by the legislature of Ontario to do business under provincial charter. They sought Dominion legislation through this House 'notwithstanding that some of us who were the friends of municipal rights and who were following in a way the lead of Sir James Whitney, protested. We did not succeed but we went on record. I think I can recall that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), who was then leading the Opposition, on more than one occasion joined with us in protesting against this invasion of provincial and municipal rights. Those of us who were then in the House pledged ourselves that when a new government came into power that new government would affirm that these rights should be protected. A new government came into power in 1911 and we expected that from that time on, in some way, the wrongs that had been inflicted by this Parliament upon municipal and provincial rights would be corrected. I am a firm believer in the principle that for every legislative wrong there 
is a legislative remedy. I have been waiting for a good many years to see that legislative remedy applied but it has not yet come. Rights, municipal and provincial, not only of Ontario, but of other provinces have been invaded by this Parliament and they are being invaded by this Act which has come to us from the Senate.
When I look into the composition of the Senate I find that the majority has been appointed by the present Prime Minister who happened to be in Parliament when these raids were made and who was associated with us in the battles of the municipalities of Ontario. That brings up this important reflection and it is a vital question before the people of Canada to-day, that the people are subject to the legislation of an irresponsible body, especially at a time immediately following our declaration in the great war that this W'as an age of democracy. Why not have democratic institutions in this country to maintain the democratic rights of the people as set up by the legislation of the provinces? I am not making any reflections upon the Senate because the Senate is a portion of the Parliament of Canada but under the conditions which exist to-day this irresponsible Senate is invading the rights of the municipalities not only of Ontario and .British Columbia but of all the other provinces. I am here to protest against the rights of the provinces and of the municipalities being subject to the acts of an irresponsible body like the Senate. In England to-day there is great agitation and legislation is now being drafted to make the House of Lords-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order; the hon. gentleman is wandering away from the subject under discussion.
Mr. W. F. (MACLEAN:	Bowing to the
decision of the Speaker, may I ask: Where am I to have an opportunity of discussing (this matter except on an occasion of this kind? I still maintain that the rights of the provinces and of the legislatures have been invaded and that it is the duty of this House to at leaslt affirm what those rights are and to see that they are vindicated. I will vote for this measure but when I do vote for it I vote for the restoration of the vested rights of the provinces and the municipalities.
We have heard a lot about the vested rights of capital. I am here to uphold the vested rights of the people and of the municipalities. I do not like to be told in this House, as we have been told, that a section of the Parliament of Canada is here for the

express purpose of protecting vested rights, meaning thereby the rights of corporations and of interests. There is no clause in the British North America Act that I am aware of which allows any part of the legislative machinery of this country to be 'considered as the guardian of vested rights. Yet, that is what we are told in this House time after time. We are told that we must accept the views of others with regard to a question of this kind. In a democratic age, at this time when the rights of the public are being assailed, this House ought to see that those rights are protected and, once for all, an answer ought to be given to this challenge, which has been issued to the people of Canada, under the auspices of the present Administration that vested rights must be protected as against the municipal and provincial rights of the people.
The people will not stand for that in this democratic age. We have got to have democratic institutions right through the whole system of Government and whoever undertakes to tell the people what the law ought to be, whoever assumes that attitude, ought to be responsible to somebody, and ought to have what we call to-day a mandate to do that. Have those who are invading municipal rights a mandate to invade the public rights as they are being invaded? I would like to see that mandate. The only mandate I can see is by going through the list of those who are invading municipal rights, to find out if I can, how the right to protect vested interests originated and where it came from.
I am sorry to say that I find that the great bulk of those who are invading these provincial and municipal rights have only one mandate, and that they happened to get from the leader of the Government. And I want to call his attention to this fact, that he will have to satisfy the people that any one in this: Dominion has the right to invade provincial and municipal rights. Our whole political activity depends on the right of holding public meetings, and wherever there can be self-determination of questions by the people they ought to be settled in the special locality to be affected. But instead of having, as in the old days, the right of municipalities to regulate their own affairs, or to have them regulated for them by the provincial government, for some reason or other that right has been transferred to Ottawa and made a matter of Dominion legislation, and our statute-book has been overloaded with legislation dealing with provincial rights. And something worse than that has happened. We have had these
rights of the provinces transferred for final decision to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. I protest against that in behalf of the people of my own municipality, and I think I can protest also in behalf of the people of the whole Dominion. The jurisdiction of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ought to be limited to constitutional questions, and should not extend to the interpretation of the intention of a municipality or of a legislature at any particular time. These ancient rights of the common people to administer the affairs of their own municipalities have been most unjustly invaded by this Dominion under the leader of the party that professed to champion provincial rights. Those rights are now being invaded by men who say they are the champions of vested rights. And they are being still further invaded by a court of appeal sitting across the Atlantic, which cannot be conversant with the questions involved in the same way as our own courts must be. The net result will be that hereafter when the provinces pass any legislation dealing with municipal rights they will insist on putting in a clause, and I think they will be justified in doing so, that the only courts to which a reference can be made as to what constitutes municipal rights shall be the courts of the province concerned, or possibly the Supreme Court of Canada. But it should not be the case, and again I repeat it, in this democratic age and after this war, as President Wilson justly said, " to make the world safe for democracy," that our provincial and municipal rights should be at the mercy of corporate influence. The world is not to-day safe for democracy, because the common rights of the people have been invaded by men who say they are the champions of vested interests, and whose only mandate, as far as I can learn, happens to be the fact that they are the appointees of the Prime Minister for the time being. And again I want to tell the leader of the Government that while he and others stood up in this Chamber years ago to defend the rights of Ontario when they were being invaded, that those rights are being further invaded now by men who sit in another place merely as appointees of the Government.
I conclude by simply saying, that while I will vote for this measure, because in a way it will get us the rest of the Act, which contains many good clauses that are absolutely necessary for the enforcement of public rights in connection with the railways, I do regret that this method has been adopted and that this House should be

called on to ask an irresponsible body to join with us in protecting public rights. I would also urge that the final court for the interpretation of the every-day democratic rights of the people o>f (Canada-their municipal and provincial rights, (should not be a court sitting four thousand miles away- a court that is not conversant with our local conditions nor with the problems that we have to solve-. We, the people of this country, should settle these questions, and settle them right, and all we aSk is that opportunity be given our municipalities and our provincial Governments to settle them. We repudiate any interference on the part of this House-although we grant that the House is now trying, in a way, to get back these provincial rights-and we protest against the way these rights have been invaded, and are being invaded, by an irresponsible body, and by the interpretation of a tribunal which, to my mind, has no right to be the final court of appeal in regard to what these rights are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend in the address which he has just delivered has wandered over a considerable field, and I know he will pardon me if I do not follow -him for the moment with respect to any suggestions concerning the abolition of the House of Lords, or of the Senate, or the limitation of appeals to the Privy Council; I would like to come a little more directly to the point. Let me say, however, that I cannot quite accept my hon. friend's view that because I have been responsible for recommending some, gentlemen to seats in the Senate during the past eight years, I am therefore also responsible for all the opinions they have subsequently expressed. I did the best I could to secure the election of my hon. friend to this House in 1911 and in 1917, but he would not expect me to hold myself responsible for every opinion that he has since advanced.
And I do not want the right hon. gentleman to be responsible for my opinions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The two cases are very much on the same lines. The position of the matter is simply this: We have been endeavouring for some few years to pass a consolidation of the Railway Act, which contains important new provisions that are eminently in the public interest-
I go further than that, and say that they are essential in the public interest at the present time. That Bill has been defeated on two previous occasions by a difference

of opinion between this House -and the Senate with regard to' the very matter that has been discussed by my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat). I do not pretend for .a moment to criticise, or to take exception to, the views which have been put forward by him or by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) with respect to the preservation of municipal rights. I entirely .agree with the view that municipal rights ought to be preserved and protected from corporate influence wherever that might be exercised to the public detriment.
But the proposal of the Minister of Railways which is now submitted for the consideration of the House is designed to save this Bill from defeat at a time when it is urgently needed, and also to preserve the existing law, with respect to the matters discussed by my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) exactly as it would have been if no amendment had been made. But more than that, the proposal is to introduce immediately a Bill-and the measure is already prepared and ready for introduction- to carry out the wishes of the House in respect of the powers conferred upon this company, and the Minister of Railways has pledged the best efforts of himself, and of the Government of which he is a member, to have that Bill passed both through the House of Commons and through the Senate, so as to give effect to the desire of the House with respect to this question. Therefore the question is simply this: Are you ready to separate this question-which concerns powers already conferred many years ago upon a particular company, and as to the elimination or limitation of which there has been a marked divergence between the House of Commons and the Senate for three years-are you willing to separate that question and deal with it in a separate Bill in order that a measure such as this, eminently necessary in .the public interest at the present time, may be passed and may not fail of enactment for a third time?
I cannot see that the situation will be detrimentally affected, from the standpoint of the municipalities, if this proposal is accepted. On the contrary, there are many important provisions in this Bill, which are eminently in the interests of the municipalities. And is it not wise that the House should give effect to this important provision, and then do its best in a separate measure to bring about the realization of the opinion and desire of the House upon ' the motion proposed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mowat)? I hope that hon. members will realize what the situation would be if

this Bill were defeated. I doubt very much whether the railways of this country can carry on for another twelve months if this Bill fails to pass, unless we introduce a separate measure into the House for the purpose of enabling the Board of Railway Commissioners, and in the last analysis the Government, to preserve the railway rates at a figure which will permit the operation of railways in this country. I hope that will be borne in mind by hon. gentlemen when they come to consider the proposal of the Minister of Railways. Let me summarize the situation again for them. Here is a measure which has twice failed of enactment by reason of a marked difference between the Senate and House of Commons which concerns the powders conferred many years ago upon a particular company. I start out -with that premise. One might say that the matter in dispute might have been dealt with in the first instance, altogether apart from a general Railway Bill. It was not so dealt with and it has been included in this Bill. We find after every effort made to bring about an arrangement between the Senate and the House of Commons that no such arrangement can be made upon the basis proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat). Well then, is it an unreasonable thing that this House should be asked to give effect to an enactment which will be of enormous advantage-to the municipalities of the country, and which otherwise would be in the public interest, if at the same time we pledge ourselves as we do pledge ourselves, that the particular question of the power conferred many years ago by this Parliament upon this particular company shall be taken up immediately by the Government, that a Bill for the purpose indicated shall be introduced into this House, and that we shall do our best to give effect to that Bill? That is the proposal, nothing more and nothing less, and I hope that hon. gentlemen in considering the course which they will pursue will realize the very great responsibilities that will be involved in the defeat of this measure for the third time.
Has the Prime Minister any assurance from the leader of the Government in the Senate that this new Bill will pass during the present session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I have not been able to obtain any assurance. I have done my best, apart altogether from the conferences between the managers of this House and the managers of the Senate, to bring about some arrangement which would reasonably satisfy the views of one side and
of the other, and I regret very much that up to the present time my efforts have been in vain.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale was submitted a few moments ago, it had the appearance of being a negative, but upon examination it appears to be negative only in part. I would direct the attention of the House and ask it to pay careful attention to the wording of the motion as it would stand if the amendment of the hon. gentleman prevails:
