That this House do not insist upon the amendment to clause 374 but that the following amendment be substituted therefor:
That clause 374 be struck out of the said Bill, and that this House insists upon the amendment to clause 374 regarding electrical power distribution in municipalities, and clause 376 regarding increased compensation to be paid by rural telephone companies.
In my judgment, the most which could be said for the motion as amended would be that it was an expression of opinion by this House. It must be borne in mind, however, that we are dealing with a specific clause of the Bill which will be incorporated into legislation and become law, if it prevails. Therefore, it seems to me that the amendment, while the verbiage might be permitted to pass on technical grounds, is not one which ought to be incorporated in the Bill. I am in the judgment of the House in this matter, but I submit that for the reasons I have indicated the amendment is not such as the House ought to entertain.

I am sure in view of the statement made by the Prime Minister we appreciate the seriousness of the situation which confronts this country to-day as a result of the attitude of the Upper House with regard to legislation which has been passed by this House on two different occasions. The question is as to the advisability of omitting from the Bill two very important clauses which concern the province of Ontario possibly to a greater extent than any other province, and as I happen to come from a constituency in which is located one of the telephone companies which is the most directly affected by clause 376, I do not feel that I can in justice to the people whom I represent, permit this matter to pass without giving expression to my views. When the question came up in Committee in this House some time ago, I explained the situation with regard to the telephone companies affected by this clause which permitted the

exaction of a penalty from any company entering into competition with the Bell Telephone Company.
I endeavoured to make that clear at that time. I consider it is not fair that the interests of these small companies should he sacrificed in this way in order to enable part of this Bill to be passed by both Houses of Parliament. The Prime Minister has pointed out that the Ministerof Railways (Hon. J. D. Reid) has pledged himself to use his influence to have a separate Bill passed by both Houses. But what prospects are there for carrying a separate Bill, provided that it is left out of the whole Bill, when the Upper House will go so far as to defeat a measure which the Prime Minister states emphatically is essentially in the public interest, as he doubts whether the railways of this country can carry on for twelve months unless this Bill is passed or certain portions of it are passed. I consider the gravity and seriousness of the situation to be such that we should not omit from this Bill certain clauses in order to enable the Upper House to defy this House which is responsible to the people of this country, and also to penalize the weaker companies that have been and are struggling under a great handicap in competition with a great company which has received franchises, not only from this Parliament, but from every province in the Dominion of Canada. The situation is such that even for the sake of doing something to relieve the railway situation in this country, we should hesitate before omitting these two clauses, and we should have an understanding whether we are going to have a responsible Government or an oligarchy rule this country in the future. We have witnessed great reforms and changes in Canada during the past few years. We have submitted to being defied on numerous occasions by the Upper Chamber-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman is not in order in calling in question the action of another House in respect to legislation, nor is he in order in discussing the question of Senate reform on the motion before the House.
Do I understand 1 am out of order in discussing the telephone question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is out of order in calling in question the action of the other Chamber in respect to legislation. He is also out of order in discussing Senate reform or anything akin to that on the motion that is before the House.
IMr. Sutherland.]

I do not intend to discuss the question of Senate reform, and if I have left that impression on the.minds of the members of the House, I am very sorry indeed. What I was endeavouring to make clear was this, that we should not subvert our opinions and what we consider to be in the interest of this country in deference to any other body, but that we should endeavour to legislate to the best of our judgment, and that we should not depart from our views on questions of this kind in deference to any other Body.
I want to point out just what is happening in the county of Oxford, part of which I have the honour to represent. Many years ago the Bell Telephone Company obtained a franchise and was exercising it in a limited service to the people in the way where the greatest profit could be obtained. As a result of their attitude, local telephone companies were organized throughout the province; and in that particular vicinity the Ingersoll Telephone Company extended their branch line out into the surrounding district and established a central office in the town, the consequence being that the citizens of the town, realizing the facilities for getting into communication with the surrounding districts, also adopted the Ingersoll telephone system in that town. The result was that there was direct competition between the two companies in the town. Finally legislation was passed by Parliament compelling the long distance companies to give long distance connection with local companies. That was made imperative, and as a result of that legislation, the local companies were enabled to get long distance connection with the Bell Telephone Company, but not only were the users compelled to pay long distance rates, but there was a surcharge oi ten cents per message collected from them in addition to the usual long distance rates. Therefore, it will be seen that the long distance telephone company suffered no injustice as a result of the legislation passed compelling them to co-operate with the local companies. What happened ? We find that, instead of dividing up the surcharge of ten cents per message with the local companies, the Bell Telephone Company retained seven-tenths or seven cents, the local companies getting three-tenths or three cents. The company I have reference to, the Ingersoll Telephone Company, maintains two long distance operators; they have their own exchange office, so that this entails no expense whatever on the Bell Telephone Company. In fact, it is a matter of convenience to that company, because they connect

with the people in the country and bring business to themselves. But these words including compensations if any have been inserted in the Bill, and they compel that company and other companies, similarly situated to pay, in addition to the surcharge, a tax or penalty of $300 for being a competing company in certain districts. We talk about monopolies in this country. If this is not the grossest and most glaring monopoly I have ever heard of, I do not understand the English language. Here is a company that has had the advantage of a wide franchise which has refused to render to the public the service which the people are entitled to receive on account of this franchise having been granted to the company, and after these local companies are by necessity forced into existence and have had to spend their money in this way, legislation is passed to compel the central company to give long distance connection, and then, in addition to the surcharge of ten cents per message, you want to penalize these companies by making them pay $300 a year additional, which means that, on the first 10,000 messages originating in the local company, the latter obtains not one cent of revenue, and after that the big company retains seven-tenths of the whole. The matter is so unfair and unjust that it should have received some consideration in the Upper House. I understand no debate whatever took place on it there, but these words were simply inserted in the Bill again. I want to point out further that, as a result of the business that is done over the Ingersoll Telephone Company's line, the Bell Telephone Company reap a great benefit by reason of their long distance connection. The figures for the two years 1917 and 1918, as regards the regular tolls collected on all calls are $10,361, plus a total surcharge of ten cents per call or $3,552, making a total of $13,913, of which the Ingersoll Company receives $465 and the Bell Company $13,448. I do not intend to take up any more of the time of the House at this stage of the session, in view of the fact that the matter has been very fully discussed on a previous occasion, and hon. members are fully acquainted with it. But I consider this is not fair, it is doing small companies a very grave injustice, because it appears impossible to have any Bill containing these two clauses passed by both Houses of Parliament under present conditions.
Sir SAiM HUGHES: What privileges are conferred on the local companies on account of this $300?

Nothing at all
This is simply a penalty imposed upon them for daring to compete with the other company. They receive no rights, no advantages, and, as a matter of fact, many local companies, outside of those centres where there is competition, are linked up with the Bell Telephone Company under an arrangement by which the latter provides the operators instead of the local companies doing so, 'but are not charged one dollar by the Bell Telephone Company because they are not in competition with that company. Which goes to prove that the $300 is simply a penalty imposed in cases where local companies are competing with the Bell Telephone Company. If we are going to encourage monopolies in this country; if we are going to give big corporations an opportunity to squeeze out business enterprise and initiative in this country, and to create monopolies we are taking the proper course in permitting this Bill to go through in this way.
I am not going to say anything regarding the features of the other clause which, to my mind, is so unfair and unjust to the municipalities of this country, because it means that, because of a certain Bill that was put through Parliament on a previous occasion, municipalities are forever deprived of their right to exercise control over their own streets, and that a big corporation is enabled to exercise those rights. If an injustice of this kind has been done to municipalities of this country in the past, that is no reason why such an injustice should continue for all time. We hear a great deal about violation of contracts and 'breach of faith and that sort oi thing. I do not think that applies in this particular case at all. We remember how, for instance, the Grand Trunk railway, years ago, received a charter from this country but by reason of the fact that rates were controlled by Parliament through the Railway Board, it is just a question whether Parliament should be equally morally responsible for the old Grand Trunk finding itself in the position in which it is to-day, outside of their association with the Grand Trunk Pacific. I mention this just to show the inconsistency of the arguments that have been advanced on numerous occasions. I do not like the idea of these two clauses being omitted from this Bill, because I know there is no more possibility of getting the two Houses of Parliament to pass them in a separate Bill than there is for a good many other unlikely things to happen. We should assert our rights as representatives of the people in this

Parliament, and we should not submit to anything of that kind by an impossible body.

I wish to add just a few words
to the statement made by the hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) regarding the Bell Telephone Company and their rates. We have been and we are asked in this country to-day, and we are having a committee endeavouring to see whether we can cut down the cost of living. :Yet at the same time we are asked in this House to pass legislation to place a further burden upon the necks of the people.
The Bell Telephone Company was granted power by the Board of Railway Commissioners to increase their rates 10 per cent, and as I understood that increase it was to be in connection with their long distance rates. But what has happened? As soon as they received this power they cut a melon; they issued so much more stock to their stockholders, and at the same time we were told that the Bell Telephone Company could not exist unless they were allowed to increase their rates. In the town of Dun-das, in which I live, we formerly had a business connection with the city of Hamilton for $45. We thought that the increase of 10 per cent would bring that service up to $49.50, but perhaps the House will be surprised to know that we were asked to sign up a contract with this poor corporation that cannot exist under present conditions, but must have a 10 per cent rate increase, not for $49.50, but for $170.50. We also had a service known 'as the house service, which cost up $30, but now we are asked to pay for this same service $148.50. You may say that we can go to the Railway Board, but I say that we should not permit such legislation to be passed. Why should we say that it is absolutely necessary to have in the Bill the words " compensation, if any?" My experience with these corporations-and I have had a good many fights with them in connection with the electric ring, and I am prepared to fight them to the last ditch-has taught me that they are well able and quite prepared to look after their own interests without Parliament intervening and putting them in a position where they can take away the rights of a municipality. I think we should consider well before taking any such action.
I doubt very much if the Government realize what we are doing when we are putting in the hands of corporations the vast powers they have to-day. I agree with the Prime Minister-I said so at the time

when the Railway Act was under discussion -that as far as the Electric Development Company of the city of Toronto is concerned, there should be a separate Bill so that we would have an opportunity of fighting the case out on its merits. I still maintain that that is the proper course to pursue, but I want to impress on the Government and this Parliament that the people of Ontario in particular are sick and tired of this cry of vested rights; we are absolutely sick of it. We have heard a lot about this " electric ring " and the Bell Telephone Company, but I am satisfied that if a private telephone company were established to-day in the town from which I come the Bell Telephone Company would not seek to put these rates in force. They would do just exactly the same as the Cataract Power Company did. They would meet the competition and the people of Ontario would reap the benefit. I strongly urge Parliament and the Government to think carefully before they enact legislation such as this, which will put another yoke upon the necks of the people.
Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and
Queen's): It seems to me there is a danger of the House being under .a misapprehension as to what is the issue upon which we are invited to vote. Hon. gentlemen opposite-J do not include the Prime Minister, with whose remarks I largely agree- have discussed questions which in themselves are very interesting, indeed, but they do not happen to be the questions upon which we are about to give a vote. I might agree with my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) as to the abolition of the appeal to the Privy Council; I might agree, I say, but this is not the time to discuss that. I agree also that there may be some need of Senate reform, but we are not called upon to deal with that here. I do not agree with the conclusion which the Senate has reached, but I do maintain that in taking such a step they were acting entirely within their constitutional rights, for if we are to have a Senate that is to be a mere echo of the House of Commons, without liberty to think and act and vote for themselves, the quicker we get rid of it the better.
My hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) discussed the old question of the conflict between the Toronto Power Company and the city of Toronto, or putting it a little more broadly, if you wish, the municipalities of the Dominion. That is not the question before us now. We have had that question before us on ^several

occasions, and we are going to have it before us again under the procedure proposed by the Minister of Railways.
Here is the position. We have before us a ponderous Bill of the highest importance, ninety-five per cent-indeed, I think I may say ninety-nine per cent-of which is in harmony with the wish of Parliament, the Senate and the House of Commons, and yet for three years we have been blocked in the carrying of that Bill because there is a difference of opinion as to the other one per cent. Now the Minister of Railways takes the very sensible view: "We do not ask you to pass judgment upon this power question; we will separate the ninety-nine per cent upon which we are all agreed from the other one per cent, and get that ninety-nine per cent through; then we will bring up the other question in a separate Bill and we will be absolutely free to discuss it on its merits." There is a homely proverb that half a loaf is better than no bread, and surely ninety-nine per cent of this Bill is better than no Bill at all. I am afraid that what is going to happen now is that by refusing to follow the course advised by the Minister of Railways we will simply be repeating the difficulties of the past; the Railway Bill will be blocked and the public affairs of the country will be seriously embarrassed.
I think these questions should be separated. I do not understand that the Minister of Railways is asking us now to decide on the merits of any one of these questions. He simply says: "We will get the 99 per cent on which we are all agreed through, and we will bring in a separate Bill dealing with the other one per cent, and the House will then be able to deal with that question on its merits."

I was going to discuss that very same point. I agree entirely with the proposition of the Prime Minister so far as the power clause is concerned, and if I could come to the conclusion that that proposition would enable us to deal with the telephone clause in the same way I would have no objection whatever. I am inclined to think that a great number of members of this House are as much interested in the telephone clause as in the power clause, but as the matter now stands before the House clause 374, which is the power clause, is being reserved, but there is no reservation of clause 376, which is the telephone clause. If that be so, and we vote for that proposition, we would be voting in favour of clause 376, or in other words in favour of 264
the action of the Senate regarding compensation in respect of telephone companies, which is the very thing a great many of us cannot see our way clear to do.
I do not want to take up the time of the House in discussing the compensation feature; I would like to have an opportunity of doing so at the right time, but I do not want to be put in the position of assenting to this proposition which reserves the power clause only, and then later on, if I desire to make a reference to the telephone clause, to be met with the objection that by assenting to the proposition of the Minister of Railways I have already agreed to clause 376, the telephone clause. I would like to have that made plain.
It has been suggested to me that under the Bill to be introduced by the minister regarding the power clause we can discuss the telephone clause, but it seems to me it would be rather late to discuss that after the House had concurred in the action of the Senate as evidenced by the joint report presented to this House. I would like to ask the Minister of Railways if there will be any opportunity not only of discussing the matter but of taking some effective action regarding the telephone clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The motion proposed by the Minister of Railways did not touch section 376 at all. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Parkdale did touch both 374 and 376. If the motion of the hon. Minister of Railways should pass it would then become necessary Jo propose another motion with regard to 3*6.
I understood that the ruling was that the motion of the hon. member for Parkdale was not in order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I submitted that it would technically be determined to be in order, but that it was not such a motion as ought properly to be entertained by the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think there is some clerical error with regard to the place at which the amendment should be inserted.
I have been discussing the matter with my friend the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle).

Perhaps I might be permitted to explain how the difficulty has arisen in which we find ourselves this afternoon. On Wednesday evening the Minister of Railways gave notice that to-day he would move that the Clerk do carry back this Bill to the Senate and acquaint their honours that this House insists upon the



amendment made to clause 325 of the Bill, the amendment having been agreed to at the free conference between the two Houses; that this House does not insist upon the amendment to clause 374, but has substituted therefor the following amendment:
That clause 374 be struck out of the said Bill, and that a consequential amendment be made to clause 462' by adding after the words " the whole " in the first item in the table of repeals therein the following words:-' except section 247 in so far as that section applies to any person or company having legislative authority from the Parliament of Canada to acquire, construct, operate or maintain works, machinery, plant, lines, poles, tunnels, conduits or other means of receiving, generating, storing, transmitting, distributing or supplying electrical or other power or energy but not including a railway company or a telegraph company or a telephone company '; and that this House does not insist on its amendment to clause 376.
Now the House vfill observe, or at least those who have been present during the entire day, that in his procedure to-day the Minister of Railways has departed somewhat from his intention as declared on the evening of June 25. He has divided his amendment into three parts and instead of moving his proposed resolution he proposes three resolutions each being an enacting clause of the Railway Act. ^It is not necessary that I should now discuss this morning's resolution in reference to 325. In regard to section 374, the motion moved by the Minister of Railways this morning is that this House do not insist upon the amendment to clause 374 and that another amendment be substituted. In the event of the House adopting the suggestion, the new clause 374 will become a clause in the Railway Act, and would not be a clause in the notice to be carried by the Clerk of the House to the Senate. It was as a result of this change, to which I believe the attention of the hon. member for Park-dale was not directed, that that hon. gentleman's amendment appeared so inconsistent. In moving his amendment, the hon. member for Parkdale assumed, and proceeded on the assumption, that the Minister of Railways was moving in its entirety the resolution of which he gave notice, as an intimation to the Senate of the desire and intention of this House. Therefore in moving, as the member for North Parkdale did, that all the words after the word " that " in' the fifth line of the resolution should be struck out, he had reference to the typewritten resolution handed to us on the evening of June 25. Taken in conjunction with the resolution moved this morning, that is, the second resolution in respect of clause 374, the hon. member for North Parkdale's 
amendment becomes quite inexplicable, because the suggested amendment should not take place after the word " that " in the fifth line, but should be made after the first " that," which was the " that " in the fifth line as proposed in June by the Minister of Railways. Of course, the Minister of Railways not having given notice to the member for North Parkdale of his intention to substitute these resolutions, possibly the same in effect but different in phraseology the hon. member for North Park-dale assumed no doubt that the minister would proceed with the resolution of which he gave notice the other evening. The Minister of Railways, in the resolution he now has before the House, has departed from the amendment of which he gave notice on June 25, by not dealing at all in the present motion with the telephone clause. I read to the House a moment ago the amendment as proposed by the Minister of Railways the other evening, the last few lines of which read:
not Including a Tailway company or a telegraph company or a telephone company; and that this House does not insist on its amendment to clause 376.
But the motion of the Minister of Railways as it is now before the House stops at the .word " company," and makes no reference whatever to the telephone issue, which I suppose he intends later on to move as a separate resolution. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

I think I have made the situation clear to the House. Clause 325 of the Railway Act was dealt with by the motion moved by the Minister of Railways this morning, and in reference to which the Prime Minister has given notice to the House that he desires its unanimous consent for the purpose of adding a further amendment or variation. The clause now before the House for consideration is 374, commonly known as the power clause. But the amendment of the hon. member for North Parkdale deals not only with the power clause but with the telephone clause, in reference to which the Minister of Railways tells us he intends to propose a subsequent resolution. To clear the air, 1 think it might be wise if the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale would at least go so far as to strike out from his amendment all reference to the telephone clause and take it up when the Minister of Railways moves his subsequent resolution. Even then, as I read the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale, in view of the present resolution of the Minister of Rail-

ways, it would practically mean that his amendment would be a blank negative of that of the Minister of Railways and would therefore appear to be out of order. Coming however, to the meat of the issue, I quite appreciate everything that the Prime Minister has said and he has stated the facts correctly.
If the Senate and the House do not agree on section 374 then the Railway Act will in its entirety fall to the ground. I am not disposed to differ from those who would say that it would have been better probably, in its inception, if the whole controversy in connection with the Toronto and Niagara Power Company charter had been introduced by special Act but in 1917-I think I am correct in the year- the then special railway committee presided over by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), when the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Cochrane) was Minister of Railways and Canals, brought into this House a Railway Bill in which the rights of the municipalities were protected to the same extent as those of us who are arguing to-day for protection desire. That Bill did not become law owing to the fact that the Senate, in 1917, refused to accept it as it came from the Commons. This year a special committee, presided over again by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), brought in a recommendation in reference to the power clause practically diametrically opposed to the recommendation brought in by the special committee in 1917. The committee of 1917 laid down the doctrine that no matter what the rights under any special charter were, no power transmission or distribution company hereafter should have the right to erect transmission lines without the consent of the municipality, or in the event of that consent not being obtainable, as to transmission lines without the concurrence of the Railway Board, they should not have the right to erect any distribution plant in any municipality without the consent of that municipality. This year's committee brought in a recommendation that the same law should practically apply in reference to transmission lines hut they took from the municipalities the right of controlling absolutely their streets and the distribution of electricity within their municipal boundaries.
There is a good deal to be said, I admit, for what the right hon. the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) urges- that is that these matters should be considered separately from the General Railway Act, but I do not think that any member of this House should be blinded as to what that means. It means that those of us who have been arguing for municipal control within municipal boundaries are going to fail, and signally fail, in our effort to secure what is desired. You ask me:	Why are we going to fail? We are
going to fail for this reason: If the House adopts the suggestion made by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) the General Railway Act will pass and there will be a clause-clause 247 of the Act of 1906 -incorporated, in so far as it is applicable to light, heat and power companies. The incorporation of that clause will prevent any company that has not got a special charter from entering upon the streets of any municipality without the consent of the municipality being obtained, although a transmission, or a distribution and transmission company, may have its rights to construct a transmission line determined by the Railway Board. Power over any distribution system for which legislative authority has been obtained will be retained by the municipalities. All companies having special charters, such as the Toronto and Niagara Power Company have, will go absolutely scot free under the amendment suggested by the Minister of Railways. The Minister of Railways admits the correctness of my argument by stating that he is prepared to introduce into this House a special Act dealing with companies that have the power to which I have just directed the attention of the House. The very object of the introduction of such a measure is to curtail and' restrain such companies as they would not be curtailed and restrained by the legislation that he has now before the House.
But what is going to happen? For the sake of my argument-I am now leaving out altogether everything in reference to the telephone business-let us assume that the Senate will accept the resolution in reference to the power clause proposed this afternoon by the Minister of Railways because it is a compliance with the law as it is to-day and in no way affects the controversy that has been before this House for some years past. But if the special Act that the minister proposes should be introduced, and which the Prime Minister refers to, is introduced into this House, and if it gets the concurrence of the majority of the members here, then goes to the Senate, the Senate will kill it because there is no reason why the Senate should give its concurrence to a clause restricting the powers of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company

when that restriction is embodied in a private Act, when they would not give their concurrence to the general Act. '
Where will the House of Commons be and where will the champions of municipal rights be? Worse than that, where will the municipalities be? I am advised by those who say they know that there is no other such charter in Canada as that which is possessed by the Toronto and Niagara Power Gompany, that there is no company with as wide powers and that this company's exponents will allege that they have the right from the Atlantic to the Pacific for all time to enter any municipality for the purpose of distributing power without the consent of that municipality having been obtained.
I see the difficulties that confront the Minister of Eailways. I see the difficulties that the railways may be confronted with in the next year, in the event of the Railway Act not passing, but I see also the difficulties that are going to confront the municipalities concerned by the charter of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company in the event of this House not securing the concurrence of the Senate in the special Bill to be introduced by the Minister of Railways. If that Bill does not secure the concurrence of the Senate, then municipal rights, in so far as the Toronto and Niagara Power Company is concerned, are absolutely negligible. The question we have to ask ourselves this afternoon is this: Are we, confronted with the (difficulties that face the railways, to take the responsibility of saying to the Senate: Unless you pass this Act as we have sent it to you, the responsibility is taken by you if the railways find themselves in difficulties? Or, are we so overwhelmed by the difficulties that will confront the railways as to say that we are prepared to assume the responsibility of perpetuating the alleged rights and privileges of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company? The question is: Are the rights of the municipalities to be sacrificed that the rights of t'he railways may be aggrandized?
For years I have stood as the champion of municipal rights. For years I have believed, as I believe to-day, that no company has the right to go into the streets of any municipality, without the consent of that municipality, for the purpose of distributing light, heat or power. I quite agree that in reference to a transmission line, it would be radically unfair that any one municipality should have the right to prevent a great undertaking being carried to 
a successful conclusion, merely by saying that the company shall not have the right to run their line of poles for transmission through that municipality. I therefore quite agree with the power that is vested in the Railway Commission of saying that such a right may be given for the purpose of transmission alone; but I am not prepared to go the length of saying that a similar right should be granted in regard to distribution.
There is only one question, as I see the issue, this afternoon: Shall this IHouse, by accepting the minister's recommendation, with the possibility, yea, the probability, if not the actuality of the Senate inevitably killing the Bill that he will introduce, confirm the Toronto and Niagara Power Company in the parliamentary powers that it has for the distribution of light, heat and energy? It is too great a responsibility for me to assume, and, as a member of this House, I am prepared to take what responsibility there is of saying, that we do not go back on the position taken here on the night when the vote was taken,-that this House should require the Senate to state whether or not they think their judgment so much better than the judgment of this House, responsible to the people, that they are prepared to hold up this measure for another year. I quite agree with what the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) has said, that it would be useless to have a Senate that never differed, even on principle, with the House of Commons; but I think it is equally useless that we should have a House of Commons that submits tamely, and without asserting itself, when it believes that the rights of the people are being trampled upon by a Chamber that is not responsible to the people.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL: Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a few observations, largely to reinforce the remarks of the Prime Minister and of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens. As has already been explained by the Prime Minister and tersely put by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, the issue before the House this afternoon is not the question of our attitude towards municipal rights on the one hand, or corporate rights'" on the other, but it is: How can we preserve the railway legislation, which is so important, and make sure that it gets through this year, and at the same time give proper consideration to the power question bv a separate Bill?
Let me remind the House of the situation. The Government in 1917 introduced

the Railway Bill into this House. This House passed that Bill containing the clause which the Senate has rejected; the Senate rejected it, and the Bill failed. It has 'been said before, but I come back to it again because it lies at the very basis of this proposition, that after months of labour spent by the two Houses the Bill failed. Last year the Union Government took the responsibility of again introducing the Bill with the clause the House desires protecting the rights of the municipalities. The Senate again struck it out, and the Bill again failed. This year for the third time the Bill went up to the Senate with this provision; the Senate struck it out again. I was one of the members appointed by this House to confer on this question with the managers of the Senate. I am quite sure there will be no difference of opinion among hon. members present that the reports presented to this House correctly represented the attitude of the Senate. The hon. senators affirmed their position and disagreed with the position of hon. members of this House. There is not any question whatever, I believe, in the mind of any member of this House who formed part of the conference that if the House reaffirms its position, and the Bill goes back with this clause in, it means that the Bill fails this year, because the Senate will not accept this amendment. That is the issue we face. My hon. friend (Mr. Nickle) speaks of municipal rights. I am just as strong a believer in municipal rights as he is, and I am just as strong a believer in public ownership as he is or any other member of this House. But what is the fact? If the Bill fails these company rights continue unlimited-if the Bill fails this company wins.
Mr. NI'CKLE: Temporarily.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It wins as long as the Bill continues to fail. And all the company desires is that the Bill should fail. In the meantime the public interest suffers because we have not the necessary railway legislation. While I am on this matter I want to draw attention to the fact that the report of the conference which appeared in the Toronto Globe of yesterday, and which indicated the attitude of members of the conference, is not in accordance with what took place. The conference was confidential, and therefore I cannot discuss the details. But the Globe report of it is not correct, nor is its statement of my attitude on this question when I voted some time
ago on the amendment of the hon. member for Park dale.
When this question came up in this House Some days ago we were called upon to vote on the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale. The Minister of Railways intimated to the House at that time-as the Government know from past experience and the best information that we could secure-that the amendment then proposed would not be accepted by the Senate. The Government could not get it through the Senate. The passage of the amendment meant that the Bill would be held up. Then what was the right and reasonable thing to do as common sense men? To try and propose an amendment which would protect the municipalities as far as possible and which at the same time might receive favourable consideration from the Senate as a reasonable compromise; or in other words to try to reach an understanding, if possible, with the Senate in connection with the matter. I voted against the amendment of the hon. member for Park-dale because it meant that the Bill would fail again. I favoured the amendment suggested by the member for Shelburne and Queens or that of the Minister of Railways because I hoped the Senate might accept such an amendment and thus save the Bill and at the same time limit and control the rights of the power company and the interests of the municipalities. My hon. friend said: Leave the responsibility on the Senate. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is a duty on the Government to try to secure the necessary legislation under which the transportation interests of this country can be protected and our railways carried on. Suppose transportation should be dislocated during the coming year by reason of the failure of this Bill, who would be 'blamed? The Government of the country would be blamed.
The Senate.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Government is blamed for all troubles now. The Govern-men would be blamed-
No, the Senate.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-in that, it did not pass a Bill which both the Senate and the House are agreed upon as vital for the protection of the transportation interests of this country. We would be told that we should not have permitted this Bill to fail because we could not agree on these other matters. The proposal of the Minister of Railways is simply to divide the Bill in two. As my hon. friend for Shelburne and

Queens said, let us get through the matters on which we are agreed, and then disicuss this other question of the power clauses. Personally, I am absolutely opposed to any corporation having the right to go upon the streets of any city at its own sweet will.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am quite sure that the House of Commons did not intend to give that power; but whether it intended to give it or not, I do not believe at this time and under present conditions any corporation should have that power. But I believe I am acting in the interests of the municipalities, as well as in the interests of the country, when I seex to help get this Bill through in the interests of controlling transportation in Canada, and then to fight out the issue fairly and squarely on the power clauses. It seems to jpe that that is the right thing to do.
What reason has the minister for assuming that the Senate will agree to the principle in a private Bill that they have repeatedly negatived in a public Bill?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the first place, it is not a private Bill, and it is not simply a public Bill, it is a Government measure introduced and backed with all the force of a Government anxious to put it through. I have no reason to assume that the Senate's attitude will be different in the one case from what it has been in the other. It may be that we will fail. If we fail what is the difference in the two cases? If we fail we are no worse off, so far as power companies are concerned; and we have put this Bill through and secured our necessary railway legislation.
What is the attitude of the leader of the Government in the Senate on this question?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not read the report of the Debates in the Senate. I know what the attitude of members of the Government in the conference was and I know what the attitude of the members of the Government in this House is in reference to this matter. We are trying to save the railway legislation and at the same time protect as far as this House can do so the interests of the municipalities.
The question of an amendment to the Senate's constitution has been discussed, and I am not going to refer to it now, except to say this: I was one of the Liberals who believed that the platform of 1893 should have been carried out and the Sen-
EMr. Rowell.]
ate reformed, and I am impenitent enough to still believe in that policy. I believe that in the interests of good government in this country and in order to safeguard the transportation interests of Canada, the Government is doing a wise and proper thing in seeking to save this railway legislation from being wrecked once more by a conflict between the two Houses. That is the object of the amendment introduced by the Minister of Railways.
If the leader of the Government in the Senate, who is a member of the Cabinet, takes a position against this proposal, what is the Government going to do?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman is in order discussing the attitude taken by any member of the Senate.
I have finished my question if the minister will only be good enough to answer it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the question is in order.

Clause 374 oi the Consolidated Revenue Bill, as amended in the interest of the municipalities, passed this House a few weeks ago, by a substantial majority, after a debate which occupied an entire afternoon and evening and was protracted until two or three o'clock the following morning. The Bill then went to the Senate and the Upper Chamber, notwithstanding the action of the direct representatives of the people, chose in their wisdom to amend the clause in question. Now the issue is once more back in the popular Chamber and surely the House which reached a decision, after such a prolonged debate, is not going to change its position to-day and allow the Senate amendment to prevail? I am oon-vinced that this House by a large majority will reject the clause in the form desired by the Senate. Surely the voice of the ^ people, as expressed through their direct representatives, should be given some consideration by those who are not directly responsible to the public, and an effort made by them to give effect to the popular will, although in the case of several measures recently the Upper House have not chosen to meet the wishes of the people, but have preferred to exercise their own views irrespective of what the people desire. Rather than give effect to the popular will, the Senate has decided to protect this exploiting company. This is not a Bill which affects the city of Toronto alone;

all the municipalities throughout the Dominion are interested in it; but Toronto will be more seriously affected than the smaller municipalities will be. Still the principle involved applies to the small municipality as well as to the large city, and in my opinion the interests of the whole of them should be protected. Surely it is not asking too much to require this company to get the permission of the municipality before entering, digging up the streets, planting poles, and otherwise destroying the appearance of a great city which has expended many thousands of dollars in beautifying its thoroughfares and creating a desirable place to live in. We know that the Mackenzie and Mann Power Company are one of the greatest money leeches that ever existed, and they have exploited every government that ever held office in this country for a period of forty years. Parliament is not asked to take away the rights of this company but only to grant power to restrict certain of those rights in the public interest.
The municipalities propose that except as to through transmission lines, where the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners is necessary, the company shall not have the right to construct or operate distribution systems on the streets of any municipality without their consent. Under the Dominion statute of 1902, chapter 107, the Toronto and Niagara Power Company claim power was given to them to construct and maintain lines of wire, tunnels, and conduits at any place through, over, along or across any public highways in the Dominion of Canada, independent of municipal control or regulation, thereby depriving the municipality of their rights to regulate or control such highways. Surely it is a serious proposition to say, or to think, that a company of this character can plant poles, construct conduits, make tunnels, and in other ways, as they choose, destroy the property of a municipality without first getting permission or without being restricted as to how the systems shall be placed through the streets of a city. When the late Mr. E. F. Clarke and Mr. Osier proposed a clause to specifically protect the interests and rights of the municipalities, it was by common consent held to be unnecessary, as it was understood at that time that the company should be subject to municipal control. No such rights as the Privy Council has held to have been conveyed were dreamed of at that time. There is not a company on the continent of North America which will have the power that this company will possess if this Bill is enacted in
the form in which it has passed the Senate. And it must be remembered that this company, as everybody knows, has been the greatest exploiting concern in America. They have made millions of dollars by the exploiting of franchises. As regards the acquisition of this company's railway and electric light system, and their subsidiary companies, even if that were done, the fact that they derived millions of dollars by the purchase, it is a hundred to one if they still would not have something prejudicial to the municipality up their sleeve. That is the danger to be feared in any dealings with them. It was thought at one time in Toronto that we were getting rid of them, but it was discovered later that they still had some other proposition which barred the way. That is why I say it is dangerous to have anything to do with these exploiters. We are nervous and suspicious even in attempting to transact business with them, because they have not only exploited the people but they have exploited the Government, and they have so many things on the side that we do not know when we are safe or when we are likely to get rid of them. Therefore, notwithstanding the action of the Senate, I hope the majority of this House will adhere to the attitude which they took a few weeks ago, and remain solidly united on this question in the interest of the mass of the people of this country.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to speak at any length at all, but I should like, from this side of the House, to emphasize the statements made in one particular, at least, by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). If the amendment of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) carries, the friends of the municipalities may just as well make up their minds now once and for all that they are surrendering the rights of those municipalities, and that the House of Commons is surrendering to the Senate of Canada. That is the one bald fact that, in my opinion, stands out, and while I think that what the Prime (Minister has said about the desirability of the Railway Bill passing find what he has said about the ^necessity for passing that Bill, is all perfectly true, and while I appreciate the plausible arguments with which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has supported the statements of the Prime Minister, I think that those who are the real friends of the municipalities should bear that one fact in mind. The one practical result, after you brush aside all other arguments, will be that a separate

Bill, providing for the curbing of the powers of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company has no chance whatever of passing in the Senate. With all due regard to what was said about the passing of the Railway Bill, I consider the rights of the municipalities to be just about as important as anything else that is embodied in that Bill. The President of the 'Council attempted to make a strong point out of this. He assumed that the Railway Bill, if it includes this clause 374, will be defeated in the Senate, and that thereby the clause itself and the purpose of the municipalities will be defeated. In my opinion the chances of the Railway Bill passing, with clause 374 protecting the rights of the municipalities inserted in it, are better than those of any separate Bill protecting the rights of municipalities passing the Senate. With regard to the rights of municipalities, I speak as a member coming from Western Ontario, and not from the city of Toronto. I think many of the members on this side of the House are rather prejudiced in the matter because they feel this is the case of the city of Toronto. But if this clause is struck out it means in effect that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company will have the right to go upon the streets of any other municipality; for instance, those of Kitchener, Guelph, Stratford, Brantford and others, with power to rip up our streets, or erect their poles without the consent of the city. Lay down this one principle-and there is absolutely no getting away from the justice of it- that every municipality should have supreme control over its own streets. That principle is destroyed by this Bill.
I want to add just one thing further, namely, that when the statement is made that vested rights would be interfered with, that certain bonds issued by this company would depreciate if this clause were inserted and the powers of this company curbed, il do not for one moment believe that those bonds were sold on the strength of any franchises which might be held in any towns or any cities outside of the city of Toronto. That being the case, I do not think these cities and towns should be subjected to the control of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company.
The one thing I rose to impress upon the House, if I might presume to do so, is simply that the practical effect of this motion if carried, no matter what explanation is given by the ministers, will be to play into the hands of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, or in other words, Mac-
kenzie and Mann, and the rights of the municipalities will be sacrificed.
This House will probably pass the separate Bill, but it will surely be killed in the Senate.
The hon. member has pointed out what will happen if this amendment carries, but in case it is rejected, will that not put the municipalities at the mercy of the Hydro-Eleotric Power Commission?

I would answer to that, as I did the other day when a similar ques

tion was asked, that I do not think any company whether it is the Hydro-Eleotric Power Commission of Ontario or any private concern, should absolutely control the streets of any municipality. Those rights should be inherent and should remain in the municipality itself. There is, however, this distinction to be drawn that the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario is owned by the people of Ontario; by the municipalities themselves; it is a public concern, whereas this is a private corporation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we are probably washing time. By the motion moved by the Minister of Railways, we are not prejudicing the position of those who are opposed t*o the Toronto and Niagara Power Company.
As I understand it, the only two questions in contention are the power clause and the telephone clause. The Minister of Railways by his resolution proposes to take the power clause out of the general Bill and put it in a separate Bill. He also proposes to put the telephone compensation question in a separate Bill. It has been argued that if we do that, we shall be killing the rights of municipalities. I take it just the other way. The Senate are holding over our heads that they will refuse to pass the general Railway Act if we do not consent to their amendment. I say that if we separate these two questions from the general Bill we shall be putting absolutely upon the Senate the onus of refusing to pass the Railway Act. If they refuse to pass it without these two clauses, the effect would be that for three successive sessions they have refused to pass an Act which is essential to the welfare of the people of this country and to the proper operation of the railways of this Dominion. But I have no doubt that the Senate will pass the Act if we separate from it these two contentious clauses, and then we shall have accom-

plished something. If we do not separate them, we shall not accomplish even that much. If we transfer these questions to a separate Bill I cannot for the life of me see why we cannot then argue exactly the same questions, have exactly the same issues before us, and accomplish exactly the same purpose, and we shall at the same time be able to pass the Consolidated Railway Act, which we have failed to do for three years. In that way we put the onus directly and squarely upon the Senate, and if the Senate, when we have a separate Bill and a separate issue, chooses to exercise its prerogative, there will be an expression of public opinion in this country such as I think they would not be able long to resist.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move that this House do not insist on its amendment to clause 376. The House will remember that in moving the previous amendment I moved to strike out the whole of clause 374, and I stated that I would bring in a separate Bill. I was in the position to strike out the whole of clause 374 for the reason that it referred entirely to the power question. This clause, 376, contains provisions with reference to telegraphs as well as telephones, and therefore I am not in the same position to move to strike out the whole of the clause and introduce a separate Bill. In moving this motion, I do not wish the House to understand that I am really approving of the action of the Senate, but I am anxious, indeed, I feel it is important, to get this legislation through at this session, and the only way in which I am likely to secure the passing of the portions of the Bill that would go through if these amendments were adopted, is by the motion I am now moving. I have no hesitation in saying that in introducing the Bill to amend this Railway Act, I will include in it an amendment striking out the objectionable words if the House desires, the same as in connection with this power question.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
If I did not move this, the Bill could not go through, because in this connection there is also a deadlock. I am just as strong an advocate as any other hon. member for the protection of municipal rights, and as I understand section 247 of the old Act, so far as the power question is concerned, the municipalities are protected in every way, the Toronto and Niagara Power Company being the only company that would not come under the Railway Act. I think that every hon. member will agree with me that the municipalities are protected in every way from any company in existence except the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. Personally,
I think that their rights should be limited. Their powers, I believe, are greater than they should be, but I could not take upon myself the responsibility of tying up the [Sir Thomas White.!
transportation of this country by any action that would prevent this Act from going through. It is all very well for the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Niekle) to say, "Let us keep this deadlock going." We can say to the Senate: "You are responsible for the railway companies going into liquidation and closing down, the railways being unable to operate as a result of the legislation not going through." But after all, I think it will be realized that the responsibility would rest on the members of this House and, of course, on the Government if we took the position of allowing this deadlock .to continue, for the railway companies of the country would shut down because they could not possibly operate it this legislation were not passed. We have been carrying on the operation of the railways under Order in Council passed by virtue of the War Measures Act, and if peace is signed within a few days, the Order in Council will cease to be effective, and we could not carry on operations without this legislation. When I introduce this Bill I am prepared to offer an amendment so far as the particular words are concerned and the House can discuss the matter. Hon. members who were on the committee will remember that we had representatives from all parts of this country asking us to amend this particular clause 376 with reference to telephones, and very important amendments were suggested in the interests of municipalities and in the interests ot provincial-owned telephones. There were amendments of great importance, and I think that by accepting this Bill as it is now we are getting very greatly improved legislation. I would therefore suggest that instead of continuing the deadlock in connection with that clause we should pass the clause and get the Bill through. While it is possible that the Senate might throw it out, we are in a position to fight that issue, and I believe we shall get better results than having a fight on this particular Bill. I am strongly of the opinion, from the fight that is being put up, that the struggle between the Toronto and Niagara Power Company and the municipality will come to an end probably within a few months as a result of arrangements that they are trying to make in order to arrive at an understanding and have the company taken over by the Hydro-Electric.

I am opposed to the action of the Senate, but in view of the statement of the minister that he will incorporate in the proposed Bill regarding the power trouble provisions dealing with the words that are objection in subsection 7 of section

376 "including compensation if any," I am prepared to support the motion, and these words can be discussed at the proper time.

I understood the Minister of Railways to announce to the House that some proposal is before somebody which will remove this opposition by 'the disappearance of this company. I do not know whether I am quite right in that or not but I hope it is the case and that in so far as this special company and municipal rights are concerned, we have heard the last of it. I also want to refer to some remarks which have been made in the course of the discussion on the previous clause and which are pertinent to this matter namely, the conflict between the two Houses. I have been told that this is not the time nor the place to discuss these things. I have been for a long time a member of this House and I have helped, in my own humble capacity, to get some progressive measures through Parliament. But you never get anywhere unless you discuss these questions when they come up. You cannot have an academic discussion as to the rights of the two Houses in connection with legislation; you have to do it as the issue cqmes up. We have been told about the responsibility for certain things that have oocurred in this country and I propose to raise again now, the question of the responsibility of the Prime Minister and the Government as to the creation of senators and other bodies in conflict with the rights of the public. That question must be solved. I have heard the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) say that they are in favour of Senate reform. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; I must rule that the subject of Senate reform cannot be discussed on this motion.

I understand
the minister's motion to be that we do not adhere to the position that we have taken in regard to the telephone clause. Will the effect of that be that the proposal of the Senate will become law and that we will be consenting that the clause providing for compensation, if any, shall be put in? I voted against 'compensation to the main telephone company. I did so because I felt that they should not get any compensation other than that which they derived from the increased business. The rural company builds its own line, it pays
the expenses of the connection with the Bell Telephone company and the customers pay ten cents extra for every message on account of getting the advantage of the use of the long distance line. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am perhaps not as. familiar with this question as some hon. gentlemen in this House. In so far as I have followed the question, it resolves itself into this: In subsection 7 of section 376 of the Bill as passed by the Senate, this language is to be found:
The board may order the company to provide for such use, connection or communication, upon such terms, including compensation if any, as the board deems just and expedient, and may order and direct how, when, where, by whom ,and upon what terms and conditions such use, connection, or communication shall be had, constructed, installed, operated and maintained.
This House struck out by amendment the words " including compensation, if any, and the Senate persists in refusing to accept that amendment. I would call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that this language does not give an absolute right of compensation. It merely confers power upon the Board of Railway Commissioners to allow compensation if the board deems it equitable that there should be compensation. It is left absolutely and entirely in the discretion of the board as to whether there should be any compensation, and if so, what amount should be awarded. The Minister of Railways proposes that we should not persist in our amendment, but he adds that he proposes, in order that the question may be raised again, in view of the strong feeling in this House on the subject, t@ include in a Bill which he proposes to introduce, a clause striking out those words " including compensation, if any," in order that the question may be taken up again at this session between this House and the Senate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am in the same position as my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). I spoke for the amendment of the House of Commons striking out the words " including compensation, if any." I do not wish to recede from that position now, because I think it is right. The right hon. the Prime Minister was not here at the time we discussed the matter, but we took the ground then, and I am prepared to take the ground now, that the words are not necessary at all. The power to give such remuneration, reward or compensation to

the main company as may be advisable can be exercised by the board, in my judgment, without these words being there at all. My objection to leaving them in arises from the fact that by leaving these words in we are suggesting to the board that it is a legitimate subject for consideration and that they would have the right perhaps to think that it was open to them to grant compensation. It was largely for that reason that I voted 'against it, and also because in my judgment, it was mere surplusage, to mention it at all. I was in favour of striking it out. I understand this motion to be that the Senate's idea is to be restored and that the Bill is to be the same as it was when it came from the Senate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But we will raise the question in a new Bill which is to be introduced.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
An argument has been put forward by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) this afternoon which, I think, comes in here. He says that if the Senate refuse in this Bill to leave out the words " including compensation, if any," by what logical reasoning, if any, can we suppose that they will leave them out when the matter reaches them in a separate Bill ? If they think it is necessary to include those words in this general Act, have we the right to suppose that they will not follow the same course in regard to this-separate Bill ?
But I wish to be enlightened upon a question of procedure in connection with the effect of this conference. We passed a motion appointing our managers; the Senate did the same thing. Those managers met and agreed' upon a certain line of action. I may be all wrong, but if it were left t* my own common sense I would say that that is the end of it so far as this Bill is concerned, because we have delegated powers to this body to deal with the subject, and I would regard such a conference as being entirely useless if we pay no attention to the decision it arrives at. I have not given the matter very much thought, but I would like to know what the Minister of Railways or the Prime Minister has to say upon that phase of procedure, which is new to us in this House. Personally, I do not recollect another conference since I have been a member.
Mr. J. A. iS EXSMITH (Peterborough East): Mr. Speaker, I have taken very strong exception to this clause, and- I regret very much that the hon. minister has seen fit to practically accept the Senate amendment. I feel that, for the moment, the Bell 
Telephone Company has to a certain extent defeated the representatives of the people. The hon. minister, of course, has promised to reintroduce the question in another Bill. Well, I have little hope of the success of that Bill when it does come before the Senate.
The Bell Telephone 'Company secured a charter some years ago which enables them to erect telephone poles and wires on the highways of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. They have a complete monopoly in the long distance business. Up until 1905 they had to a great extent refused to give people in the rural parts a telephone service-at least, they put their rates so high as to render the service practically prohibitive. As a result all over the province of Ontario and in parts of the province of Quebec private and municipal telephone companies sprang up, and in 1906 the Bell Company were forced to give connection to those companies. The Railway Commission at that time, I think, decided that the Bell Company should receive some compensation. I have here the rates that some of the rural telephone companies pay for compensation. Take, for instance, the Home Telephone Company, operating in Markham, Pickering, Whitby, Brooklin and Port Perry. This company has somewhere in the neighbourhood of a thousand subscribers and1 pays, first of all, $300 as compensation, which the Bell Telephone Company acknowledges covers all the switching and overhead charges and everything else. But despite that fact the Bell Company also ask the Home Company to pay another 10 cents on every long distance message from its subscribers. This Home Telephone Company, with its thousand subscribers, transits free to them all the long distance calls that come from the Bell Company, but when the Home Company's subscribers ask for a long distance call they are charged an extra ten cents, of which the Bell returns 3 cents to the Home Company. I think it is absolutely unfair for the Bell Company through their monopoly to be able to prevent all rural telephone companies competing with them, and I do hope that the Minister of Railways will have the promised Bill before the House at the earliest possible date.

At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. Newton W. Rowell (President of the Council) Bill No. 158, to provide pensions to or in respect of members of the Canadian Naval, Military, and Air Forces, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

The subject dealt with
by this measure was referred to a special committee which has been sitting quite a long while, and has been at considerable pains to come to right conclusions. When a matter is referred to a special committee, members of the House generally do not know as much about it as those who form the committee. I think it would be well to have a general explanation of the committee's recommendations as embodied in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Possibly my lion. friend was not in the House when the resolution upon which the Bill was founded was moved. I then gave an explanation of the general provisions of the Bill and the changes from the existing pension regulations. That all appears in Hansard.
It is all right.

If I am in
order, I would like to make a few remarks in regard to this Bill.
This is not particularly in the way of criticism for I think, as the minister said the other day, that the Bill, while not being all that every member of the committee desires, does represent in a fair degree what may be called the substantial conclusion of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. As I understand it, the hon. gentleman desires to debate the entire Bill. If that is his intention, I must ask for him the unanimous consent of the Committee, because otherwise his remarks would be out of order unless they were confined to the clause under discussion. Is the unanimous consent of the Committee given for the hon. gentleman to debate the Bill?
Carried.

I was about to say that I think it is my duty, on behalf of the soldiers, to bring to the attention of the Committee one or two things which are not particularly embodied in this Bill, but which should go hand in hand with it. In the first place I think this House and this Government are justified in recognizing the medical examinations of their own medical officers. I believe that any soldier who joined the Canadian Expeditionary Force, who was fit for any risks and was passed as medically fit by the officers of this Government, should be so considered and that no pre-enlistment disability should be marked up against him from any cause whatever. Another point is this. It appears to me that there is a discrimination against the unmarried man. The principle of the Bill, of course, recognizes giving pensions to women and children. Probably I can best illustrate my point by giving an example. Take two boys who joined in 1914 or 1915. One of them took occasion to get married at that time, the other decided to postpone his marriage until he returned. The first would be entitled to $20 a month separation allowance as well as the patriotic money that his wife would draw during the whole time that he was away. The second one, returns to this country, probably with the same dis-

ability as the married one. The married man gets a pension and his children also, while the second one, according to the provisions of this Bill, does not participate in the benefits of the pension fund. I think that is a discrimination of an unfair character that this House should not allow.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will my hon. friend mention that last point again, as I did not follow him?

Two boys start out in 1914 and join the Expeditionary Force. One gets married. His wife would be entitled to separation allowance and to patriotic money. When he comes back, if he is wounded, his wife gets a pension. The other one, who would be in the same position, decided to postpone his marriage until his return. He comes back with the same disability, and when he gets married his wife gets nothing. I think that is an unfair discrimination and one that should be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is not correct in his statement. If the second one marries on his return his wife will get the same pension as the other one who had been married before her husband went overseas.
I am glad of the correction; I read the Bill the other way.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I imagine what my hon. friend has in his mind is this: In the event of the second returned man dying his widow would not get a pension, whereas the woman in the first case would.

That at least covers half of my point. I think it is unfair. But the main thing that I want to bring to the attention of the Committee- it does not exactly pertain to this Bill, although it should accompany it-is the condition in regard to insurance. I have been informed by the Pensions Board that out of 60,000 of the boys who were drawing pensions from this Government, about 20,000 cannot get insurance. I have visited many of the hospitals and sanitariums throughout the country and I find that is a thing that is worrying them very much. They have wives and families, they have no means except the small pension which this country has given them-and I must say it is small in spite of the raise which we are giving them-and they are not able to get insurance that will provide for their families when the stage of dissolution comes. I think it is the duty of this country to re-

store these boys to the position in this respect that they were in previous to enlisting. That means that the Government should pay the difference between what it would now cost them to carry insurance and what they would have paid before joining the army. The department of insurance here informs me that the average cost of insurance per $1,000 for a man twenty-five years of age is $14 and odd cents. That is, of course, shorn of all unnecessary expenses. This insurance up to a limit of $5,000 per man would cost about $70 per year. Granting that to the 20,000 sub-standard lists which are at present among the casualties, assuming that their risks have been doubled, would only mean to this country $1,400,000 per year of expense. I do not want to ask the country to give them something for nothing. I think it is only right and fair that they should pay the same amount that they would have had to pay if they had not been injured, but that the difference between that and what they have to pay under their present disability should be borne by the country. I know that there is a great strain upon this country at the present time, and I realize that the Government are anxious to avoid all unnecessary expenses, but I think this is a duty that the country really should assume. In connection with that, I would like to point out that there is in this country about $40,000,000 worth of enemy property. I think it would be only just and fair that the Government should take that property, capitalize it, which would give an income of about $2,000,000, and use it to pay for the insurance on these soldiers. That would relieve this country of the financial burden, it would give the soldiers the insurance that they want and must have if their wives and children are going to be left in decent circumstances, and the country would be discharging its obligations. I hope the Government will give that serious consideration in the near future.
I would like also to draw the attention of the Government to conditions on the Pension Board. We have been informed that there are about ten thousand complaints a month. I think any organization that cannot regulate its business in a more satisfactory manner than that would indicate, cannot be reckoned as an efficient organization.
