And I think that all the high offices on that board should be occupied by men who have seen service. I find that some twelve or fifteen men drawing salaries of $5,000, $4,800, $3,000, and so on, were
never in uniform. I have nothing to say as to why they were not, but I do say that in any soldiers' organization in this country, such as the Soldiers' Re-establishment Board and the Pension Board, you will never have conditions satisfactory so long as you have the highest-paid officials men who have never served their country in uniform. I daresay these gentlemen are efficient officers-I have no complaint as to that-but I think they should give way to men who have seen service in France. Now, the insurance problem deserves very serious consideration. It is one that is worrying the soldiers who are so badly disabled that they cannot get insurance to protect their wives and children, and I submit that this House and the Government should give the subject careful attention in the very near future.
I just want to say-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the unanimous consent of the Committee that the hon. gentleman have leave to continue the general debate?

I believe that insurance for returned soldiers is one of the most vital questions that you will have to deal with. A few years ago insurance was looked upon as being more or less a luxury, and a man was considered prodigal if he put much insurance on his life; to-day life insurance is an absolute necessity with men who have no other means of support for their families. Yet we find, as the member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) has said, that invariably where a man is suffering from any disability which would make him a pensioner under this Act, he is refused insurance by the insurance companies, or, if he is allowed insurance he has to pay a very high rate. I do not think the amount required to make up the difference between the insurance rate demanded of these men and that demanded of ordinary healthy men would amount to anything like the amount spoken of by the member for Muskoka. But no matter what the amount may be, insurance is vitally important to the disabled man, and I think it is one of the things that this Parliament should take up in the very near future, if it cannot be dealt with now and under this Bill. We find that a man who ordinarily can get life insurance for $30 or $40 a year will in many cases be asked to pay $40 or $50. We had the same experience with men who had insured their lives before the war; when they went overseas they were asked by some of the companies as high as $100 ad-



ditional on a very small policy on account of war risks. And the same is true today. I think the Government might work out a scheme for insuring these men. I have no desire to force on the Government a scheme whereby all soldiers should be insured; my proposition is that where men are desirous of taking out life insurance to protect their wives and children they should be at no financial loss on account of their condition after coming back from the war. This matter, of course, only affects those men who come under the Tensions Act, and I think the member for Muskoka has done a great deal for those men in bringing this matter forward, and it should be carefully considered by this House. I think it would be a good thing if provision for those cases could be made under this Bill.
During .the past four or five years we have heard a great deal in this House, particularly during the time of the Military Service Act, regarding medical examinations conducted in this country and overseas. In many cases we have complaints from returned soldiers saying that they were not allowed their pension, because the authorities claimed that they were suffering from some particular disability, or partial disability, before they went overseas. But in almost every case those men before going overseas were subject, not to one examination, but to many examinations, and not by the same doctor, but by different medical boards. It is quite clear to me that any man who got over to France was, in the opinion of those medical boards, perfectly physically fit. If disability did not show at that time I cannot see any reason why any part of a man's pension should be deducted for a supposed disability that he had before entering the army. This is a great cause of dissatisfaction. Then we have other cases; I have heard complaints from time to time that a man is getting too much of a pension. I believe in some cases that is right.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: But not unless he gets to France.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.

That was my point.
[Mr. Arthurs. I

That is my argument I know personally where a number of men were subjected to the most rigorous examination-perfectly physically fit men so far as I could see-and were rejected, but were taken afterwards in other battalions. So I can see no more reason why a man should be debarred from a pension on account of injuries received in England, even although he did not get to France on account of the medical examination. But my purpose in rising was to support in the strongest possible way the hon. member for Muskoka regarding insurance, which I think we should deal with at the earliest possible moment.

Soldiers are supposed to
speak with brevity, and I shall endeavour to be brief in supporting the arguments of the last two hon. gentlemen. I want to speak particularly of one question-widows' pensions. The board have recommended that a widow's pension be raised to $48 a month. I suggest that $48 a month is not sufficient to keep the widow of any of our brave fellows. Why, Sir, when I hear of the prices which ladies have to pay for their clothes, as reported to me in domestic matters, $48 a month would not pay for a hat-and we want to see our war widows in a position to live decently. It is not so much what is due to those of us who are here and are able and willing to make a living, but it is what we owe to the dependents of those men who lie to-day in unrecorded graves upon the ghastly battlefields of Flanders. I have seen many a man in an unrecorded grave in a rotten old shell hole.
Those men were on duty, too, and that is what I want to emphasize as I say these few brief words in favour of the widow's pension. I think the widow's pension should be raised to $60 a month at least, and a corresponding amount given in the case of the children. In the case also of those men who have been disabled I think the amount should be doubly raised. This great and chivalrous country does not care, and will never object, though the expenditure involved for these purposes reaches ten, twenty, or even two hundred million dollars. Even so, we must take care of the dependents of those gallant fellows who fought and died for us on the red battlefields of Flanders.	*

I should like to follow the example of other hon. gentlemen who have indulged in a general discussion of the terms of the Bill. In the first place the measure that we now have under considers-

tion, growing out of the war, is one of the utmost importance. All other claims that may be put forward on behalf of soldiers are entirely secondary to the Pension Bill. No matter what schemes the Government may have for civil re-establishment, or for gratuities, or for assistance in the matter of education, all these proposals are quite secondary to the proposals for adequate payment of pensions to those who have suffered in the war. Therefore, I agree with the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me that generally we look for an increase in the amounts of these pensions, particularly the pensions to widows and orphans and t-o those who are: seriously injured. We believe it is the desire of the country that those people who have suffered shall he placed in such a position as to be relieved from want and from the fear of want for the future, and we believe the Canadian people will support the Government in making liberal provision for such cases. We are grateful for what has been done up to the present time, but we believe there is still room for improvement. I think I may say on behalf of the soldier members of the House that we shall continue to press for recognition ,of these very just claims. It seems to me we require to- have a realization of what lies before us in the matteT of pensions. As time passes we will be confronted with problems growing out of the fact that there will be cases coming to our notice of men who suffer from other causes in the future. I give you, for instance, the case of a man who, ten years from now, meets with some terrible accident and becomes a charge upon the community. I venture to say that in that day sentiment engendered by the fact that he was a soldier and fought for his country, will be such that the public will not agree such a man should be a public charge and demand will then be made, and I think public opinion will support it, that because he was a soldier, the country shall protect and take care of him. And so it would go on, and twenty-five, thirty, or forty years from now, these men growing old and perhaps meeting with misfortune would be liable to become charges upon the community but it will be sound practice, and public opinion of that day, I think, will support the contention, that they should be cared for.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Peter McGib-bon) has raised the question of insurance. In the case of men who, by reason of their disabilities, cannot get insurance, if the Government now undertook or originated
265J
proposals for dealing with insurance of that sort, it would largely guard against the obligation which in the course of time would arise and would bear upon the public.
The question has also been raised as to the personnel of the Pensions Board. Now the transaction of public business calls for probity and efficiency, and the best men that are obtainable should be secured. But such a business as the payment of pensions, besides the highest standard of efficiency, what is absolutely necessary is that there shall be a sympathy existing between the board and the pensioners; and *we have an idea that we would get that Sympathy on behalf of the board towards the pensioners if a spirit of comradeship existed and the members of that board *were men who, to some extent at all events, had endured the same trials and tribulations and had faced the same dangers-in fact if both had been comrades together. We shall press very strongly in the future, giving the Government time to turn around and make the necessary arrangements, for the recognition of the principle that the administration of pensions should be in the hands of those who have that sympathy which we think alone can be felt by men who have been comrades and have served together.
With regard to the previous medical examination the principle contended is a perfectly sound legal principle, and I do not see how the Governmeent can get away from it. Medical officers are employed by the Government and they decide whether a man is fit or not fit. If they pronounce him fit then they ought to be stopped from subsequently saying that he is not fit. We shall press very vigorously for 9 p.m. the recognition of that sound, legal, and I think, moral principle.

In the first place I want to endorse, without discussing the proposal of the hon. gentleman (Mr. P. McGibbon) as to insurance. In my opinion it is absolutely necessary and should be very gravely considered by the Government. In connection with the pensions to widows, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) has rightly said that $40 a month, with $8 bonus for the present, is entirely inadequate. I do not know how anybody can reooncile the money that the wife of a soldier received during the war with the pension that the widow is now offered. At all times during the war the wife of a private received $30 separation allowance, $15 from her husband, and $10, or possibly slightly higher

from the Patriotic Fund. Compare that amount with the payment of $48 to a widow at the present time. I suggest to the Government that the provision for the widow for the future is manifestly unfair. There is another point that has not been given any consideration by the Government, and that is the unfair treatment of two men of equal class, one of whom does his work in Ottawa, in Victoria, B.C., in Halifax, or elsewhere in Canada whilst the other man does exactly the same work, hut goes to England or Siberia. Under this pension scheme the man who went to Siberia, which is a pretty safe theatre of actual war, and the man who went to England and enjoyed life there, are entitled to the full disability pension, if they fall and break their leg in the street, or if they receive some other disabilty not directly due to the war.
But if the man that did exactly the same work in Canada receives disability he is not entitled to any disability pension whatsoever. I think the treatment under this section is, therefore, unfair, and I commend such men to the notice of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps some explanation should be given, otherwise there would be a misapprehension in the minds of hon. members with reference to some of the points that have been mentioned. I want to present, just in a few words, the views of the committee, as I understand them, in reference to these matters. Let me take, first, the pre-existing disability. Under the law as it stood until the House met a year ago, a pre-existing disability was taken into consideration by the Board of Pension Commissioners in estimating the amount of pension. That is, if a man had some disability at the time of enlistment and the result of his service was simply to aggravate that disability, the pension commissioners would only allow a pension in respect of the aggravation. It was urged before the committee, as it has been urged here, that if the soldier passed the medical examinations in Canada and England and actually got to the front and faced fire, a pre-existing disability should not be taken into consideration.
Why should there be any distinction between the man who got only as far as England and the more fortunate one who was sent to France?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There was this distinction before the committee: A man is not entitled to a pension with respect to a pre-existing disability. In other words, the state compensates him for the 
disability sustained or aggravated during service. The state is not under obligation to compensate him for a disability which existed prior to enlistment. But the committee thought, if the Army Medical Service passed a man and he actually got to the front, we should ignore any question of preexisting disability and grant him a .pension, but if he did not get to the front they thought the law should not be changed. The committee of last year gave this matter careful consideration and that was their, conclusion.
Is Siberia a theatre of war? And is Bermuda a theatre of war?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Siberia is a theatre of war; Bermuda is not.
Is St. Lucia a theatre of war?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I presume St. Lucia would not be, but I do not recall at the moment. Last year the Committee, as I said, considered the matter and reached the conclusion I mentioned. The matter was considered this year again, and the Committee reached the same conclusion.
Let me take next the point mentioned by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Peter McGibbon), that is, the unfairness that he suggests in treatment between two men, one who married before he went overseas and the other who marries after he returned. As the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) points out, in both cases the man would get the allowance for the wife, and there would be the allowance for the children as well, but in the second case, if he marries after the disability is incurred, his widow and children would not receive a pension. May I tell the Committee why? In the investigation which was made in 1917 by the Board of Pension Commissioners and the hon. member for Kingston into the operation of the pension laws in the United States, they found that the United States are still paying pensions to widows of veterans of the war of 1812. Let me illustrate. A man twenty years old returns from overseas; he lives fifty years and then marries a girl of twenty and she lives fifty years. You have her drawing a pension 100 years after the war, and in case there are children, they will be drawing pensions too.

How does the minister make that out? In our country the wife's and the husband's years run concurrently. If I live fifty years and my wife lives fifty years, that does not make 100 years, it just makes fifty years of marriage.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suggested if the pensioner .married when he was seventy.
He marries at twenty.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He returns when he is twenty and then he lives until he is seventy. He may have had a wife or two in the meantime.
When he is seventy he marries a girl of sixteen.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
That is immoral.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There have been a number of such cases in the United States.
We cannot take that case -that is not an actual case.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the actual experience in the United States.
That could be remedied by imposing a time limit.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let me give another case which is the actual experience in the United States. The Pension Bill o-f the Civil War to-day is larger than it was immediately after the war.
It started to decrease in 1913.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it started to decrease in 1913. Let me take the case of men permanently disabled and very near to death. In the United States they have had the experience of such men marrying young women-or young women marry-them,-and the women becoming pensioners of the State for life. This question received the most earnest consideration at the hands of the committee, and the committee decided that it was not wise to depart from the sound principle already embodied in the legislation, that where marriage took place after disability, while the husband, during his life would get the benefit of the additional allowance for the wife and the children, it was not expedient to provide a pension for the widow or children after his death.
Let me now consider the question of insurance which has been mentioned and which is undoubtedly a very important matter. The view of the committee-and I think the House will see that they were correct in this view-was that it was not a matter that came within the scope of the investigation of the committee. The committee was appointed to consider pensions, and while insurance was an important question, it was not within the scope of reference made by the House to the committee.
Let me now take up the question of the employees. It is true there are some employees who are not returned soldiers. These are the figures. At the head office, there are 231 returned soldiers, and the men over eighteen years of age who haye not served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force number 39. That is, out of 270 males over eighteen years of age, 231 are soldiers. In the district offices, there are 193 soldiers as against nine males over eighteen years of age who have not served overseas. It will, therefore, be seen that the overwhelming majority of the males over eighteen years of age employed in the head office of the Pension Board here and in the district offices are soldiers and, with few exceptions, men who have served overseas.
My point was with reference to the high officials drawing big salaries.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
An answer was made in the House to the question of my hon. friend, and from this answer it appears that a certain number of men, some of them medical men, who were in the permanent force and who were assigned to this particular work from the start, are still working with the Pension Board. The Pension Board is a body created with power to act independently of the Government and they have selected their own employees subject to the Civil Service Commission. There men have acquired great experience in dealing with important problems arising in the icourse of pension administration, particularly questions of disability. The Pension Board-there are just two members at present, both of whom are returned soldiers-(believe it is in the interest of the efficient administration of the board to keep these men in their present posts. I have no personal knowledge of the situation, but the number who are drawing large salaries and who have not been overseas is limited. Members who are interested will find full information on the matter on page 3176 of Hansard.
Another question raised was that of widows' pensions. The committee had great sympathy with the position of the widow, and did make a substantial increase. The pension of the widow has been raised from $40 to $48, a bonus of twenty per cent, and for the eldest child from $12 to $15. The widow gets $48, for the first child $15, for the second $10, and for the third $8. Therefore a widow with three children would draw $81 a month, or practically $1,000 a year. That is a larger sum than a wife

with a family of three would receive if she were drawing assigned pay, separation allowance, and Patriotic Fund allowance. With assigned pay, separation allowance at its highest figure, namely, $30 a month, and Patriotic Fund, she would receive $75. So a widow with a family of three children draws more under the pension law as we have revised it, than a wife in the ' same position would have drawn while the war was on. Of course, what other countries pay is not necessarily a criterion for us, but I think what is paid in the United States should be a matter of interest to us here. Under our new scale a widow will receive $576 a year, in the United States $300; a widow and one child will receive in Canada, $756, in the United States $420; a widow with two children in Canada $876, in the United States $570; a widow with . three children in Canada $972, in the United States $6.30; a widow with four children in Canada $1,068, in the United States $690. You will see that our scale of pensions is very much higher than the American scale, so far as the widow and children are concerned.
Does the minister think we should take the United States as a model ? We did not follow thei* example in getting into the war, and I do not see why we should follow them in the matter of pensions.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I quite agree that we should not follow them. If we had, we would have reduced rather than increased our pensions. I only mentioned that as indicating that the committee had all these considerations before them, and they were pressed very ably, as they have been tonight. We had before us the rates paid in every other country, and while our pensions are perhaps not as generous as we would like to see, they are larger than are paid by any other country that took part in the war. The widow's pension in New Zealand, for instance, is $379.
But is that a fair comparison? What is the value of the dollar in New Zealand?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reason why the
United States is a fairer comparison is because the dollar is more nearly of the same value in the two countries.
Less 3 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have given the figures for the other countries simply to show what they pay. The value of the dollar in years to come will probably be more nearly the
[Mr. Rowell. I
same in all these countries than it is to-day. The difference in value is owing to conditions arising out of the war.

I am aware of a difficulty which has arisen in the interpretation of the expression "dependent condition." I am hopeful that the language of the Bill as now presented to the House will make the meaning clear. Let me state the case. It is that of a commissioned officer who was killed at an early stage of the war. His widowed mother is living. Inquiries having been made, it was found she was residing with some relatives. They were not rich people, nor were they needy people, like the average of our country people, and inasmuch as she was living with relatives who were not deemed to be needy the case was not held to come within the pension conditions. The matter was not pressed very much. As a matter of fact, the lady herself did not make application for the pension, but such inquiry as was made by others interested in her case led to the information being given that inasmuch as she was living with relatives who were not in needy circumstances the claim was not one that could be recognized. I am not putting this forward as a complaint, because the matter has not been pressed, but it would strike me that under the terms of this Bill this lady, if not possessing independent means, would be entitled to a pension under the terms of section 34.

I might mention a case almost identical with that mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding). A young lawyer in my constituency, being unable to secure a commission, volunteered as a private and went to the front. He won his commission there, but was killed in the battle of the Somme, while holding the rank of acting major. He left a mother and an invalid sister. The Pension Board granted the mother a pension, but about a year afterwards they discovered 'that she was deriving a small revenue from some real estate which she possessed, hut which revenue, she explains, is largely eaten up in taxes. The pension has been taken away from her. The hon. memb'er for Quebec West undertook in the committee to have an amendment made to introduce the word " income " in clause 34. but I believe was not successful. I have brought the case to the attention of the Pension Board on several occasions, and they have promised to give it consideration. Evidently, if this woman is not given a pension, a great injustice will be done, especially seeing that the pension was

granted for some time. In vie\v of the circumstances of the young man s death, I trust the minister will give consideration to this case.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would suggest that my hon. friend bring this matter up under section 34.

I should like a little further light on a question asked by my hon. friend from Muskoka, as reported at page 3176 of unrevised Hansard. The point was whether the large-salaried men employed by the Pension Board were returned soldiers, or men who had not worn the khaki and been overseas. I notice that the following salaries are being paid: Mr. K. Archibald, $4,800 per annum; Mr. F. C. Baker, $2,200; Mr. R. R. Belanger $1,700; Dr. D. M. Bell, $3,500; Col.
C. W. Belton, $5,000; Col. J. S. Dunbar, $4,700; Capt. W. L. Germaine, $2,600; Dr. W. O. Gliddon, $3,500; Capt. E. King, $2,900; Mr. J. Kittle, $1,700; Mr. J. C. Letellier, $1,500; Mr. N. Mcllveen, $1,800; Mr. F. T. Orgill, $1,800; Mr. J. A. W. Paton, $2,900; Mr. G. 'Sleeman, $1,600; Mr. P. Williams, $1,100. I have been informed that none of these gentlemen are returned soldiers, and I would like to get a straight answer from some one who knows what the facts are as to these officials, and whether there are any returned soldiers among the high-salaried men. Let us have the facts about the department's organization.
I am informed that none of these men mentioned are returned soldiers.
Why?

Mr. K. Archibald was medically unfit for service overseas. Mr. F. C. Baker was a member of the permanent force. With reference to Mr. R. Belanger, I have no information. Colonel C. W. Belton was on the old Military Pensions and Claims Board, as was Colonel Dunbar. Captain Germaine was a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force but did not go overseas. With reference to Doctor W. Gliddon and Mr. J. Inglis, I have no m-formation. Captain King and Mr. . Kittle were members of the permanent force. With reference to the others I have no information.

Not one of these men went overseas', and hundreds of returned soldiers in the country could no doubt be found with capacity and experience and quite the equal of, if not superior, man for man, to the men mentioned in this list.
Canada is professing to be very generous and kind to the men who fought for their country, hut if this sort of thing is to be continued it will be a direct refutation of the statement that the country is caring for the returned men. I would ask the minister to make a careful inquiry into this matter and take Ehe necessary steps to purge this department in ervery case where men can be found who went overseas and who have sufficient capacity to perform the services required of them, especially if they are equal ot nearly equal to the men who now hold places.
On section 2, subsection (g)-" Disability ":

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A portion of the definition here given of disability more properly comes in in connection with section 11. I therefore move to strike out all the words in subsection (g) except those in the first line, so that that clause will read:
Disability means a wound, injury, or disease. Motion agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 11-Pensions to be awarded according to prescribed rates:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move to amend section 11 by adding at the end of the first subsection the following:
Provided further that when a member of the forces has suffered disability or death after the declaration of Peace, no pension shall be paid unless such disability was incurred or aggravated or such death occurred as the direct result of military service.
I am transferring to this section an important part of the clause we struck out of (g) in section 2.
What is the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Under the law as it now stands, our pension system is really an insurance; that is, if a man dies from any cause during service his dependents are entitled to the pension. The view of the Committee was that after peace is proclaimed if men are kept in the service for the purpose of clearing up fag ends, etc., during peace, the insurance element should be eliminated.
On the other side too?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Either overseas or here. After peace is proclaimed the insurance element will be eliminated. The man will become entitled to pension if his disability was the direct result of service.

Suppose a soldier is kept in France with a regiment to collect the debris of the war and in connection with that work he receives a serious wound. In that case, I suppose he will be considered as having been wounded in the performance of war service.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. He would get a pension.

What the minister
means is that if while engaged in the discharge of his duties he dies a natural death, from illness contracted outside of military-functions, the provision he mentions applies?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Surely there will not be many of these cases. Why introduce that element?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Our law as it stands is broader than the pension law in any other country, so far as we know. The insurance feature which I have mentioned is not in any other law, so far as I am aware. In that respect, we give the soldier the 'benefit of insurance during the whole period of the war.
Mr. GRIESBAOHi: That is the principle that underlies all pensions.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. The principle underlying all pensions is disability due to service. Under our pension law, if a soldier contracts disease under a purely normal condition having no relation at all to service, he becomes entitled to pension. It is really an insurance system.
In what way will disease or ailment he attributed to service?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If a man contracted a disease when an epidemic broke out in camp, that disease would be contracted in service, and as it now stands he becomes entitled to pension. If he went home on leave and were taken ill at home, unless there us a special provision to change the law, he would still become entitled to a pension. The view the Committee took was that once war is over and peace is officially proclaimed, there is no longer any war risk, and we might then afford to put ourselves in the same position, as every other nation now is even during war period, namely, that the pension should be granted only in case of death or disability due to service, and in the latter of the two cases I have mentioned he would not be entitled to a pension.

On section 12-cases of intemperance or improper conduct:

We are not here to criticise, but I am sure that all hon. gentlemen who are soldiers are anxious to give the Committee the benefit of their advice. This clause says that:
A pension shall not he awarded when the death or disability of the member of the forces was due to intemperance or improper conduct.
1 think that is a puritanical distinction and that it might very well be struck out. According to that clause, a soldier who had perhaps not misbehaved himself for a long time-and I am not trying to condone intemperance-might fall and break his neck, or something of that kind might happen to him, and his wife would be deprived of her pension.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that the clause says:
*-provided that the commission may, when the applicant is in a dependent condition, award such pension as it deems fit in the circumstances.
This has been in the pension regulations from the start and was recommended by the Committee of the House three years ago.

The language of the section would seem to me to be contradictory. It begins by saying that a pension, under certain given conditions shall not be granted, and it concludes by saying that under certain other conditions it may be granted. I suppose the meaning would be that under the conditions mentioned it shall not be granted but that under other conditions mentioned the commission may take the facts into consideration and grant a reduced pension. I think that is what it must be read to mean, but the drafting is a little peculiar and contradictory.

I would of course deprecate anything that a soldier would deprecate, but the most remarkable thing in the service is that very often the worst cases are the best fighting men. Men, full-blooded fellows who would get into scrapes by giving rein to their inclinations, who would go and buy champagne, have a "little time" and perhaps suffer field punishment for it, would be the very best men we had when it came to going over the top or when any serious fighting was to be done. Any distinction in regard to men of that kind I think is liable to work a hardship on some of our very best soldiers.

The interpretation clause defines improper conduct as "wilful

disobedience of orders, self-inflicted wounding and vicious or criminal conduct." I think the clause would be satisfactory if the word "intemperance" were struck out.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the least objection to striking that out. It was put in by the Committee of the House some two years ago and has been in the regulations since. I would move:
That the clause he amended hy striking out the words " intemperance or " in the 19th and 20 th lines.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Before that section is passed I think it would be a fair thing to put in, after the words "improper conduct," the words " as defined by this Act." Then the soldier looking after his rights will be led to see what is the definition of "improper conduct." Without these words being in, I do not think the section is a fair one for the general public.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no objection to that. That is what it means now, as I understand it. I would therefore move:
To further amend clause 12' hy adding after the word " conduct " in the 20th line of page 5 of the Bill the following words " as herein defined."
Will this clause be retroactive? There may have been pensions refused to applicants on the ground of intemperance.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This law has been in force for some time. It is not a new law. If an applicant has been refused on that ground his case may be reviewed by the law as it stands. Section 48 provides:
All cases affected hy this Act shall he reviewed and future payments shall he made at the rates and in accordance with the provisions set forth herein.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

The clause gives to the Board an unlimited power. I think the intention is that they shall not give the full pension but that they may give a reduced pension if they see fit. I would take that to be its meaning. But it says that the Commission may "award such pension as it deems fit." I think it is merely a question of drafting; I have no difficulty in understanding what it means.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will quite concede that the clause might have been better drafted. The intention is that if a man is guilty of improper conduct his family shall not be entitled to a pension, but the Board of Pension Commissioners may, if his family is in a dependent position, award such pension as it deems fit in the circumstance*. I think the intention is that the board may award such pension as comes within the limits defined by this Act. We might perhaps leave that over for a few minutes and see if we can find a form of words to more clearly express the intention.

I am not objecting to the clause. I think I can gather the meaning, although I do not think it is well drafted.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 13-time within which application must be made:

Is there any good reason why this clause should remain in the Bill? According to the provisions of the Bill, a pension is due by the mere fact of disability or death on the one hand and of the financial condition of the dependents on the other. Why should a person be deprived of the right which is acknowledged by this Bill by the mere fact that the making of a claim has been neglected for a period of three years?
I would have no objection to the clause if it said that if a person does not make a claim within three years, then it shall have no retroactive effect, that is to say, the pension will be granted only from the time when it is made. But as I read the clause, it means that a person who is in a hurry to make a claim will at once have the claim considered; while if another person for some reason or other thinks that she does not want it-she may have forgotten about it, she may not know the law, she may have been absent from the country, she may have been ill, her attorney may have forgotten to file a claim-if for these or for any other reasons the claim is not made within three years, then she loses her claim. This seems to me to be altogether unjust, and I would suggest that the clause be stricken out, or, that it be amended in the manner I have suggested.

I support the contention of the 'hon. gentleman (Mr. Denis). We ought to have some regard for the period of the war. Suppose a man was killed in the early days of the war, that is more than three years ago, and owing to any of the causes to which my hon. friend has referred a claim was not made, the party not understanding the law, it would be a pity that the claim should be shut out. I would suggest to the minister that the three years might well be extended to cover the period of the war.

As t'he members of this committee will see, the claims divide themselves into two classes: First, dependency; second, disability. The Pensions Committee felt, dealing with the classes in that order, that if a person had three years after he or she became dependent in which to make the claim, it was reasonable to suppose that if no claim were made there was not dependency. I would direct the attention of hon. members to the clause in reference to each case.
A pension shall not be awarded unless an application therefor has been made within three years (ib) after the date upon which the applicant has fallen into a dependent condition;
That is, if the dependency happened five years after the war, there would be three years more before the prescribed right would prevent the applicant collecting the pension. Now, in respect to (a):
A pension shall not be awarded unless an application therefor has been made within three years (a) after the date of the death in respect of which pension is claimed.
That is, if a person is killed in the war the dependent making the claim has three years from the date of the death. It seems unreasonable to think that if any one wanted a pension he or she would wait longer than three years before making application. Then take the third case :
A pension shall not be awarded unless an application therefor has been made within three years (c) after the date upon which the applicant was retired or discharged from the force.
The object of that subsection is this: Experience has taught other nations in other wars that after a protracted period of time a great many fraudulent and fictitious claims are made, and if there is not a time limit prescribed it is impossible for those in charge of the pension administration to protect the Government, because all evidence is gone. We were strongly advised when we were in Washington in 1917 that it would be essential to specify some period of time within which claims had to be made in respect to disability, otherwise it would be impossible to protect the Government. I may say that we did increase the term from two years to three years.

In respect to subsection (a), here is a possible case of which I know there are some existing: Until this measure comes into force the Imperial widow is not recognized by our pension law. If an Imperial soldier was killed in the spring of 1915 his wife, having hitherto not been among the privileged classes, her application for a pension, the three years

having expired, could not now be entertained.

That is a very strong case. But supposing a Canadian soldier was killed in the early days of the war, and through any misunderstanding the claim of his dependents was not put forward, no matter what the cause might be, should such a claim be shut out? I grant you there, must be a time* limit, but there ought to be a time limit which will recognize the circumstances of the war. We sometimes talk of a debt being out of date. This kind of debt should never be out of date.

There are a number of Imperial widows whose husbands were killed in 1914, and they have never made application because they have never been recognized by the Canadian Pension Act. They will make application as soon as this Bill goes through. In some cases the three years have already expired. Although the intention is to give them pensions, technically speaking, under subsection (a) they are debarred.
I think that should be dealt with.
It had better be dealt with now.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the Committee thinks there should be some provision such as suggested by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), say thr'ee years after the close of. the war, I would not offer any objection as the minister in charge of the Bill. The Pensions Committee felt very strongly, however, that some limit must be imposed to protect the country from claims which might be /made in the future when all evidence to check them up was lost. If the Committee desires to insert "Three years after the proclamation of peace,"
Is not the ordinary civil debt proscribed in five years?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It depends on the laws of the different provinces. Five years after is a long time to hunt up any medical evidence as to the condition existing at the time.

I think in nearly all cases the application will be made in good time; people are not likely to neglect these things intentionally. But if any bona fide case can be shown where, through misunderstanding or absence of some one, the application was made more than three years after the soldier's death, it would be a hardship

if that case could not be considered. I do not wish to move any amendment; I am quite content to call the attention of the minister to it.

This very class ot cases have caused the Patriotic Fund any amount of trouble in its attempt to give post-war relief. We were trying to draft a clause which would protect the Patriotic Fund from claims made a certain length of time after death or disability, and we came to the conclusion that the only wa^ to do it would be to limit the making of the claim for a certain number of years after the declaration of peace, so that practically all the claimants should be on the same basis in so far as the calendar was concerned. My own impression is that it would be far better to amend that clause in such a way as to make it .three years after the declaration of peace. Then you have a definite period after which no claim can be made, and if that period is found to be too short, then Parliament could extend it.
. Mr. FIELDING:	That will cover it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then I will move that
the following be inserted as paragraph (d) of clause 13:
Three years after the declaration of peace.
The word " or " should be stricken out of paragraph (b) and put at the end of paragraph (c). Then the new paragraph follows.
What does the minister understand by the " declaration of peace?" Does he mean the signing or the ratification?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The official declaration
of peace, which brings the war to an end.
Mr. -CHARLES MARCIL:	Some people
say Germany will never ratify the Peace .Treaty, although she is going to sign it.
. Mr. ROWELL:	An official proclamation
will have to be issued at some time, bringing the war to a conclusion. The declaration of peace is referred to in other sections .of the Bill.

I have a case in mind, and I would be glad if my hon. friend could give me an answer to it. A soldier .is killed and the widow remarries, and again becomes a widow. Would she be entitled to a pension?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will come to a case
of that kind when we consider a later section.

What is the definition of " dependent condition " in paragraph (b)?
Mr. NI-CKLE:	" Dependent condition "
is defined in section 2 paragraph (e) as meaning the condition of being without earnings or income sufficient to provide for maintenance and that the resident in Canada shall be considered to be in a dependent condition wh^fi such applicant is not in receipt of earnings or income equivalent to the amount of pension provided for such an applicant.	*

Suppose one of our soldiers were in a dependent condition in the United States, for you will find them scattered all over the world in a few years, could he get his pension just the same?
Mr. NI-CKLE: I would think so, yes.

In my opinion the definition would not allow him to get it.
Mr. -NICKLE: Paragraph (e) reads as follows:
" dependent condition " means the oondition of -being without earnings or income sufficient to provide for maintenance.
That is. the bald statement of the principle, and then the following words apply to Canada:
An applicant resident in Canada shall be considered to be in a dependent condition when such applicant is not in receipt of earnings or income equivalent to the amount of pension provided for such an applicant.

Suppose the applicant is a resident elsewhere-a resident in the United States, in England, or in France?
Mr. N.ICKLE: I think that in the case of an applicant in the United States probably the same rule or standard would apply, the conditions and cost of living being about the same there as in Canada.

I am not satisfied with the amendment made to clause 13, because I do not think it is what we want to say. Three years after the declaration of peace applies to the whole clause, and I would suggest that the clause read this way:
A pension shall not be awarded unless an application therefor has been made within three years after the declaration of peace, unless, and within three years

Then come paragraphs (a), (b) and (c).
The hon. gentleman's proposal seems to be more involved.

Application must be made anyway within three years after

the declaration of peace, and it must also be made under one of these three alternatives.

The whole section as amended by the Committee reads as follows:
A pension shall not be awarded unless an application therefor has been made within three years:
Now come the alternatives:
(a)	after the date of the death in respect of which pension is claimed;
(b)	after the date upon which the applicant has fallen into a dependent condition;
(c)	after the date upon which the applicant was retired or discharged from the forces; or
(d)	three years after the declaration of peace.
The application can be made under one of these four alternative schemes within the term of three years.
Is it intended that a person falling into dependent circumstances after more than three years shall then be considered?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

He or she would come
under paragraph (b).
10p.m. Mr. FIELDING: There would be no limit in that case?

That applies to cases of
prospective dependence.
How are you going to prove exactly when a person falls into a dependent condition?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that the whole question of such dependency is more or less a difficult one. Where the pension is granted to parents or brothers or sisters with respect to the death of a son or a brother, there is no legal right to a pension. The pension is only granted in case they are in a dependent condition, and there is reasonable ground to anticipate that a contribution would be received from the son or brother towards the support of parents, brothers, or sisters, as the case may be. Now at the time of the close of the war, or five years after the close of the war, no pension may be payable, the parents not being in a dependent condition; but in case this aged father or mother, who perhaps had some little property or income, should at the end of five years, or even at the end of ten years, fall into a dependent condition-and "dependent" is defined in this legislation'-then it is still open to them to make application to the Pension Board for a pension. It
[SBr Herbert Ames.]
is really intended to protect aged parents who fall into a dependent condition.
They do not fall into a dependent condition all at once, the process is very gradual. Bow are you going to fix the date at which they arrived at that condition?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that "dependent condition" is defined, as the member for Kingston has pointed out, in paragraph (e) of clause 2, and it means the condition of being without earnings or income sufficient to provide for maintenance. In Canada that means when such applicant is not in receipt of earnings or income equivalent to the amount of the pension provided for the applicant. So that, whenever the persons who claim under the clause applicable to prospective dependency make an application, they would have to show that they were not in receipt of earnings or income within the -amount fixed by this clause defining "dependent condition." Then if they can show that their earnings are less, they are entitled to a pension.
That application can be made at the end of ten years?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Quite so.

But within three years from the time dependency exists.
Mr. ROW'ELL: That is it.

Somewhere else in the Bill it is provided that on the death of a man who was disabled between 80 and 100 per cent his widow comes into a full pension. If a man lived for four years and consequently fell outside of the three-year period after the declaration of peace, and then died, this limitation of three years after the declaration of peace would not, as I understand it, affect the pension, there would still be three years after his death in which claim could be made for a pension.

What is meant by "a dependent condition "? I know of a case where a father and mother living in the north country, had only one child, a son. The son. was killed early in the war. In a sense they have no visible support; they have a little home and a little sandy land, but the father at present is able to do only a little work, and of course, this case is not considered by the Pensions Board as one in which the parents can receive any assistance at all.
Will the hon. member let that stand until we come to clause 34?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-pension suspended on imprisonment or .paid to defendant.

There is a point in this with which I am not quite satisfied. The clause reads:
The commission shall have discretion to pay the pension to any person who was being supported by the pensioner at the time of his arrest.
After the word "being " the words " or was entitled to be " should be inserted.
" Or was legally entitled to be."-
I have cases in mind, but it is no use discussing them.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no objection to that.

I suppose it is the intention to have the commission pay the pension to any person who was being or entitled to be supported by the person whose pension is so suspended. I would suggest that the words " have discretion to " be struck out of the eighteenth and nineteenth lines. The clause would then read:
That the 'commission shall pay the pension to any .person who was being or was legally entitled to be supported ,by the pensioner at the time of his arrest.
That would leave no discretion to the commission, but would simply say that it would be the duty of the commission to pay the pension to whoever was entitled to be supported by the person who was imprisoned.	-

The pension is only suspended during that time, and it might be that the pension commissioners would desire to accumulate it and pay the entire *amount to the man on his discharge. It would not be right that any person who was being supported by the pensioner could have the right to come in and demand the money. I would suggest to the Cpmmittee that the word "legally" as suggested by some hon. member, in the amendment, be left out, because in some provinces a parent is legally entitled to support, and in other provinces, not. The commissioners might desire to pay the pension to a person who might not be legally entitled to it. It would be better if the clause read in this way:
That the commission shall have discretion to pay the pension to any person who was being
or who was entitled to be supported by the pensioner at the time of his arrest.

How is this discretion going to be made use of ? In principle I am against any discretion being given to a commission or a judge or anybody else when this can be avoided, and I have never known laws to be so unjust and iniquitous as those in which discretion is left either to a commission or a judge or any other judicial body. It is the duty of the legislature to take the responsibility of framing the law, and if the legislature is not able to determine to what cases the discretion should be attributed or in what sense it should be made use of, how is a judge or a commission going to make use of that discretion? Do we know or do we not know what we intend to do about this matter of discretion?
If we know, we should have it put into the law and if we do not know, how is the commission going to know? Or, if the word " discretion " is going to be left in, let us determine the discretion and say that in a particular case the discretion is to be made use of, and in a different case, the discretion will be made use of in a different way. If we leave the matter open for the commission to decide at their own discretion, they will not know what we intend to do, and I am sure two different commissioners determining on the same point would render a different judgment, just as, every day, different judges, when they have nothing but their discretion to guide them, judge and determine differently on points which are absolutely simple. Everywhere in our law, when the question of costs has been left to the judge, we have found all kinds of diverse opinions. If this discretion, is to remain in the law, it should be determined at-once by ourselves.

There is no department of the public service that will have to be administered more simply than the work of the Pension Commission. You cannot reach the object we really have in view without giving the Pension Commission a certain amount of discretionary power, because they would have to use it if they are really to meet the object the Government has in view. In this case, you can very easily see where discretionary power is needed and might be exercised to great advantage by the commissioners. A man is arrested who is entitled to a certain sum of money which, if he were a law-abiding citizen going about his ordinary business, would be paid directly by the Government to him and would probably through him reach his family.

If he breaks the law, the Government says: "We do not want his family to suffer; therefore, we ask that power be given the commissioners to pay money for the support of that family while the man is in jail." You sometimes have cases where the woman is just as bad as the man; there may he four or five children in the family, and if you say that the money must be given to the woman because she was receiving it while the man was with her, or because she is entitled to receive it, she might drink every cent of it and let the five children starve. The Pension Board would consider whether the woman was fit to receive it. If they decide she is, she will get it but they may decide that the children at least must be cared for while the man is in jail. Therefore, if you are going to treat that family sympathetically, some discretionary power must be given to the board.

Then the board would have to render judgment in each case of this kind, and if they are going to do justice, they would have to make a thorough investigation in order to get the facts, whereas if their discretionary powers were determined now, all the commissioners would have to do would be to follow the law.
iSir SAM HUGHES:	Would this apply
in the case of one of our pensioners who goes to the United States and gets into jail?
I would think so.
How would the commission act in the United States? How would they ascertain the merits and demerits of each case?

The Board of Pension Commissioners have quite a corps of investigators and examiners going about the country continually. They act through the British Consul in the United States, The moment the attention of the board was directed to the fact that a pension cheque was not cashed, or they received information that a pensioner was in jail, one of their investigators would at once trace up his family, make an investigation, and report back to the board for decision and action.
I think there is a good deal in the contention of my hon. friend (Mr. Denis).

From the observations made by my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) and my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) I can

quite understand that with an army of five hundred thousand soldiers there would be a very large army of dependents, and the commissioners themselves will be able to do only such work as would fall under -the heading of general work.	The
actual work of investigating	these
cases will have to be done by a large staff of assistants. That is where the experience of my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) is very valuable to the committee and the board. As the secretary of the Patriotic Fund-as the, manager, I (might say, because he had the whole works throughout Canada in his 'hands-he had assisting him, first, the volunteers who wanted to help the cause of the Patriotic Fund, and then committees of citizens and many other associations, all acting free gratis, as the Irishman says. Will the men who investigate these cases for the Board of Pension Commissioners act in a voluntary capacity? We could not afford to pay for such a large army of investigators as would be required to investigate cases of the kind that have been mentioned in all of the large centres, and in remote sections of Canada where they may have to make inquiries regarding the bona fides of the pensioner or his dependents. How are you going to organize this vast army of investigators? Will you rely on voluntary help and charitable organizations? Will it be done in connection with the Patriotic Fund? Let me put a concrete case. Suppose a pensioner in Gaspe goes to jail. The board has discretionary power to say whether or not his family shall receive his pension during his detention. Who would investigate this case? Would you apply to the minister of the church, to the mayor of the village, or to some patriotic citizen in the neighbourhood, to make a report? The administration of this Act is a very delicate matter. It also involves the expenditure of large sums of money, and we must take all precautions.
Does not my hon. friend think that a system will grow up?
No doubt, but I should like to know how the machinery will be put in motion.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At the present time the Board of Pension Commissioners has its district officers in all parts of Canada. Gaspe, which my hon. friend has mentioned, is in the Quebec district. In addition to these district officers, there are also district visitors who try and keep in touch with the families of the pensioners and visit throughout the district. In the ordinary

course, a visit would be paid at certain intervals to the pensioners at Gaspe. The board also, takes advantage of the assistance of the Patriotic Fund and in various centres has asked the committees, and will ask them in future no doubt-because I understand some of these committees are going to continue-for a report in such a case as my hon. friend has mentioned. In the absence of either one or the other,
I have no doubt they would apply to just such representative citizens in the community as my hon. friend has mentioned. In other words, they must use the best machinery available to get information so that they can exercise their discretion as intelligently and sympathetically as possible.
They will rely on public-spirited citizens?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not in sympathy with this section. A pension is not given as a reward for virtuous conduct in the future. It is something that the soldier has earned by his services to his country. He is entitled to it; it is for the support of himself and his family. Therefore, why should we keep strings on it and tell him he must go to Sunday school and church regularly and do a lot of virtuous things, that he must not get drunk and get a sentence, or he will lose his pension? I am not in sympathy with that at all. Once we say that the man is entitled to his pension why should we follow him?

I quite agree with everything the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has said: If a man gets his pension it is his property, and we should not follow him and insist on his going to Sunday school, or take it from him if he gets intoxicated. But assume that he is in prison for six months and has a wife and five or six children starving outside, and refuses to allow the Pension Commissioners to pay that money to his suffering family. Does it not seem obvious that there must be some machinery by which tfhe State will see to it that the money thus belonging to the man shall be used to maintain those whom legally he was bound to keep? I would draw the attention of the leader of the Opposition to the fact that the man's pension is only suspended if he is imprisoned for six months. His property in the pension is recognized and the man is entitled to it at the expiration of his term of imprisonment, provided that in the meantime it has not been paid to some one who was entitled to be supported by him. The
object is primarily to protect the man, and secondarily to insure that those whom he has a duty to support will not suffer during his incarceration. It is a recognition of the very principles to which my hon. friend has called attention.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The word "suspension" has many meanings. If an officer of any department of the Government is suspended he receives no salary during that suspension. I construe this to mean that the pensioner while in prison will receive nothing, his rights being suspended. It does not say that payment is suspended. If you say that payment of pension will be suspended, that is another matter; but as it stands now, the man's right to his money is gone while he is in jail.

If the intention of this section is merely to suspend payment while the man is in jail and pay it to him when he comes out, I am in accord with it. If, however, the intention is to keep the pension back altogether, then I am absolutely opposed to it. The man has earned his pension by reason of disability, and the country has no right to take it from him if he incurs the wrath of the law and is sent to prison. If that is the intention it is most unfair and I should strongly oppose the carrying of that section.
'Mr. McKENZIE:	My experience of men
who will possibly come within this class is that although a man may get drunk and be put into jail, his wife or some member of his family can reach him with a cheque that requires his signature and thus get the money. I have known of cases where men were in jail on pay-day and their wives would take the cheques to them and obtain their signatures. I do not think there should be any interference at all in this matter. If later on it happens that trouble arises in this connection, remedial measures can be taken, as Parliament meets every year. But at present I do not think we should anticipate difficulties of this kind and impose ungenerous conditions on the ' soldier.

I suggest that this be made to read:
His pension shall be withheld and not paid to him during his confinement.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The suggestion of my hon. friend from St. Antoine would cover the point and make perhaps clearer what I understood to be the meaning of the clause. However, my attention has been drawn to this consideration, which I mention in order

to get the view of the committee on it: If a man is sent up for manslaughter for ten years, should the pension continue to accumulate during that period in case he has no dependents, or should it be forfeited in view of the fact that he is maintained in a public institution at the expense of the State?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Personally, I do not think we should interfere with pensions at all. If the soldier encounters misfortunes afterwards they will he bad enough in themselves without taking away what little he earned in the better part of his days.
In any well-conducted jail he would not be allowed .to receive his money, so that he could not get it until after he got out.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Probably it would be better to amend the section. I move that in line 16 there be inserted, after the words"or more," the words "the payment of." So that it would read:
The payment of his pension shall be suspended and shall not be paid during his imprisonment; provided, however, that the commission shall have discretion,-
-and so on. That would make it clear that the right to the pension was not forfeited, but that payment was suspended and his dependents might be cared for.
I think you should make it: "paid to him."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Very well. I would move that the section be amended so as to read:
When a pensioner has been sentenced to imprisonment for a period of six months or more, the payment of his pension shall be suspended, and his pension shall not be paid to him during his imprisonment; provided, however, that the commission shall have discretion to pay the pension to any person who was being supported by the pensioner at the time of his arrest.
Why do you mention six months specifically?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the period were shorter it would not be a case for the Commission to inquire into. If the Commission _ were called upon to look into cases which were only a matter of a few weeks, they might be kept busy investigating cases.
I presume that was the view in deciding on six months.
A man's dependents might be in needy circumstances during a period of five months just as much as during six months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the latter part of the section is somewhat loose. Suppose

the pensioner was giving his money to some person who under the Act had no right to i',t at all. Would it not be better to say who the dependents would be. As dependents are defined by the Act somebody who had no business to get it might be obtaining the pensioner's money during the time he was in jail.
The commission have a discretion and I assume that in the administration of their work they would make inquiry as to the payment of the money.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is no discretion left here. It says:
That the commission shall have discretion to pay the pension to any person who was being supported by the pensioner at the time of his arrest.
Any person can come in and say that he, or she, is entitled to pension.

I would not construe the section in that way. I would construe it to mean that the commissioners would have *a discretion as to whether or not the payment should be made and as to the people to whom it should be made, and that they would only pay the pension to some person who was entitled to be supported by the pensioner.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps the previous clause settles it; that is that it shall be paid to those who have a right to be supported.

I should think so.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 18-appeals and rehearing:

This clause is peculiar. It says that:
Two or more commissioners shall sit for the purpose of hearing the appeals of dissatisfied applicants or pensioners.
That would mean that they would hear appeals^from their own decisions. In addition the clause seems to imply that the three commissioners shall give a joint decision. It is not the decision of one commissioner but the decision of the whole board when an applicant is refused a pension. It is peculiar in this, that when an applicant is refused a pension by the board, he gives notice in writing that he proposes to appeal against the decision of the board, and then he is allowed to come before the board and make his appeal to the same men who gave the decision originally.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon, friend will turn to subsection 8 of section 3, he will see that it provides that:
The approval of the commission to the award of any pension, or the refusal of any pension, shall he evidenced by the personal signature of at least one of the commissioners.
The evidence before the Committee showed that in the actual work of the board, unless there was a case involving some serious dispute, it would be disposed of by one commissioner. In a case in court where there are three judges, one will dispose of an ordinary case. So, in this case if there was any real dispute an applicant who rwas not satisfied would be entitled to have a rehearing before the full board.

Do you not think that a complicated, or complex case will, from the very beginning, be adjudged by all of the commissioners? They Will form their opinions and the soldier, or the dependent, or whoever is receiving the pension, will have to appeal before the same commissioners. It is as if we were to appeal before the same court that had rendered its decision. The court will simply confirm its judgment. Perhaps it might be possible, outside of the commission, to have a permanent appeal board.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be more like the case of an ex parte application to a judge; the evidence and necessary medical certificates are furnished by the Department of Militia and Defence to the Pension Board and they make such further investigation as they think necessary and then award the pension. If the applicant is not satisfied, he comes before the commission for a rehearing or review, in which case the applicant may be permitted to bring all the facts before the board either personally or by counsel and is entitled to a hearing before two or more commissioners. The commissioners have no object other than to do justice in the administration of the Act and the purpose of the section is to entitle any applicant to have his case reviewed.

I take it for granted
that the cases to be reviewed are complex and that in such cases the whole board will have to pass upon them. If I were a member of the board and a difficult case came up, especially in the matter of a pension affecting the welfare or happiness of a whole family, I would like to consult my colleagues.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that my hon.
friend will see that this provision is of real value to the applicant. After his case 266
has been passed upon in the way indicated upon the papers prepared in the office, he may appear in person or through counsel and have all the facts reviewed by the board of pensions commissioners whose sole object will be to administer the Act impartially.
I have no doubt that they will have that one object in view.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. If any new facts were brought out, the fact that they had decided the case already, would not prevent them from reviewing their decision.

An appeal here at Ottawa is of no value to a man living in Vancouver. He cannot pay the expense of coming to Ottawa or of hiring counsel to represent him, and he is not very much better off than he was before because he is not able to appear personally. I would like to ask if there is any expectation that the commissioners will travel across Canada and be available to those who wish personally to appeal.
One of the commissioners is frequently making trips across Canada, and sometimes two, to meet those who are dissatisfied and who ask for a rehearing.

Subsection 8 of section 3 does not distinctly give one commissioner the power to decide anything. It says that the signature of one commissioner shall be evidence of what the board have done.
I can see the logic of one commissioner deciding ordinary cases, but where an appeal is taken to the full board, the provision of subsection 8 of section 3 is not that one of the commissioners may decide it. but that after the board, persumably a majority, have decided it, the signature of one commis-board would be responsible for his decis-of that commissioner but of the board.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct. It is not that the decision of one of the commissioners is the' decision of the board, but that the decision shall be evidenced by the signature of at least one commissioner. As a matter of administration in routine matters one Commissioner would dispose of the application, but the whole Board would be responsible for his decision.
That is implied but it does not distinctly say so.
I suppose this commission, which will deal with large sums of money, will be under the control of the Auditor General ?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes; everything is under the control of the Auditor General.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
