speechtext: If the minister thinks this is to be a review it should be so stated. If it means appeal, that is covered. But there is nothing better settled, as the minister knows, than as to what is an appeal and what is a review. One has nothing to do with the other. If it is to be a review, there is a discretion to admit new evidence and the same court can hear the case again. If it is an appeal, it is naturally an appeal from one or two commissioners to some other new commissioners. It has been stated already that there should be no appeal to the person who has already decided the case; if there is to be a second decision it should be by some fresh tribunal which is free from any prejudice by reason of the former decision. In our Nova Scotia courts we have seven Supreme Court judges. They constitute the full bench, but there can never be seven judges sitting, because one of them has tried the case which is being heard on appeal, and he does not sit. We have commissioners here, and there is an appeal to them. In such an event the commissioner who has already decided the case should not be sitting on the appeal.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. minister
rather hinted that the parties may appear by counsel before this body, and it will be readily understood by lawyers that, if so, the language of the statute would at once be strictly construed and insisted upon.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 19-Assignment of right of action for damages as a condition for pension.

I do not think the section is very clear. Take the case of a soldier who is accidentally hurt, and apply that section. It reads:
If a disability or death for which a pension is payable under this Act is caused under circumstances creating a legal liability upon some person to pay damages therefor, the commission, as a condition to payment of the pension, shall require the pension to assign to His Majesty any right of action he may have to enforce such liability of such Person or any right which he may have to share in any money or other property received in satisfaction of such liability of such person.
Assuming a soldier has an accident insurance policy and is disabled. He had been keeping that policy up for years for the benefit, probably, of a creditor or of a dependent not within the class of dependents constituted by this Act. Would it be the policy of the Government to say that this man should be required, merely because he was a pensioner, to assign that to -the Government in preference to all oither persons who might have a claim upon it?

No, that is not the intention. My hon. friend will notice that it is only where there is legal liability created upon some person to pay damages, and the payment of life insurance would not be the payment of damages; it would be the liquidation of a contractual obligation.
Is that the definition in the Act?
I think the common law definition would apply.

It seems to me that this clause will take away from a soldier who may be disabled the returns of his occupation, and will compel him to elect whether he will take a pension or will take his right of action against his employer. He gets his pension for his services overseas. If he is injured subsequently while at his work he is entitled to recover from his employer, and why should the Crown ask to take an assignment of his right of action? He ought to get both, it seems to me.

Certainly.
Mr. N'ICKLE: My hon. friend is, quite right, the man would get both. The section says, "If a disability or death for which a pension is payable under this Act is caused under circumstances creating a legal liability," and so on. If the man had been discharged from the forces and had entered civil life, he would not be entitled to any pension in respect of any disability incurred therein; but if, prior to his discharge, he had suffered disability in the war or incidental service, he would be paid his pension in respect of that disability, and compensation in respect to his second disability in civil life would also be paid to him.	This clause has more to
do with this class of case: A man, while in service, walking down the street is run over by a street ear and severely injured.
He is entitled under this Act to a pension in respect of disabilities suffered. The object of the section was that the right of action could be assigned to the Crown and the person who had caused the injury could be sued in court. Then the pensioner, or the soldier, would have to elect as to whether or not he would take the pension, or take the damages that may have been recovered by the Crown as against the negligent person.

If a soldier while in the
service is injured in the manner suggested, surely he is not entitled to a pension?
266i

The pension regulations
have always been in Canada that the soldier from the time he enlisted until he was discharged, was insured as to anything that might happen to him except in relation to improper conduct as defined by this Bill.
* Section agreed to.
On section 21-payments, unclaimed instalments, pensions not to be assigned or charged, disposal of unpaid balances:

I would like to have an
explanation about unclaimed instalments and especially in regard to the words in the third line of paragraph 2:	"pension
which has remained unclaimed." Does this mean a pension which has already been granted by the board but which the pensioner has neglected to collect, or does it mean a pension for which a claim could have been, but was not made?
Mr. NdiOKLE:	It means a claim in
respect of a pension which has been granted and unclaimed for two years.

What about a pension for
which a claim could have been, but was not, made? Would such pension also be lost?	;	1
A case of that kind would be covered by section 13.

I do not see why a person to whom a pension has been granted should lose that pension by the mere fact that such person has neglected, ,for a period of two years, to collect it. I understand that a pension once granted belongs to the pensioner just as rightly and equitably as a deposit in the bank belongs to the depositor? It is money actually earned and owed by the State to a person who is named as the pensioner in this Bill. Now I am coming back to the same argument as before in respect to prescription. If for some reason a pensioner has neglected or forgotten to draw the pension-if he has been absent, or sick, or has assigned the duty to some one else to collect the duty for him and it was not done-why should that person be deprived of moneys which really belonged to him or her? I do not see any reason for this deprivation and I would like to be told what that reason is.

The Pension Commissioners advised the committee that already cheques were piling up, unclaimed by pensioners whose whereabouts were unknown, and the committee reached the conclusion that if a pensioner was able for two years

to get on without his money, it was not unreasonable that it should come back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the country. The pension was paid
11 p.m. with the object of assisting the man in his maintenance, owing to disability incurred during the war, and the purpose of the provision was to clear the administration office of these cheques which had continued to collect. There is a good deal in what my hon. friend says in regard to the money belonging to the man. That is right, but in the event of his not coming after it within two years, it did not seem unreasonable that unclaimed balances should be transferred to Consolidated Revenue account and' remain there.
Mr. DENI'S: The clause should be drafted so as to be applicable to all moneys remaining unpaid over two years. Take the man who has for twenty-three months refrained from making a claim. That man has the right to a pension for that period but if, unfortunately, he. refrains from making a claim and collecting his pension for one month more, then he loses his [DOT] pension for the whole two years.

I think my hon. friend has misread the section. If he will refer to paragraph 2 he will find that it reads as follows:
It shall be a matter within the discretion of the commission whether a pensioner shall be paid any instalment' of his pension which has remained unclaimed by or for him for more than two years from the date such instalment became due.
He would be entitled to all instalments that had not been prescribed for at least two years.
Section, agreed to.
On section 23-pensions to children, age limit, marriage, etc.:

I consider this clause a very important one, especially subsection 3, which provides:
The pension for a child shall be paid to its mother, or father, or to its guardian, or to a person appointed by the commission.
I submit that is opening the door very wide to allow the Commission, in its discretion, to deprive the parents of the right-of a pension. Let me briefly give the Commission a ease which came under my notice. A family residing outside of the city of Ottawa, the father of whom was practically an imbecile, sent three of their sons voluntarily to the front, all they had over age, there being two younger boys. Two of these

sons were killed and one boy was left still overseas. The Militia Department refused to give the mother-who was engaged in farming in a small way, her husband being unable to work-any allowance because the father was supposed not to be incapable of earning some livelihood1. They did decide, however, to give a pension for the upkeep ol the two younger children by reason of the death of the two sons. They refused to allow the mother to handle that money, which is only $16 a month, and they appointed a corner grocer to receive the money to be expended upon these two children. The Committee will readily understand the humiliation of a mother being deprived of handling the small sum of pension money for the benefit of her own children. I brought the case to the attention of the Committee, and they informed me that some fastidious person-some woman or other person whom they sent to examine into the circumstances of this family-was not quite satisfied with the mother, and therefore upon that recommendation the mother was deprived of the handling of that money.
I took it upon myself to ask two very respectable gentlemen who lived nearby to make a report in writing, one of them being the Liberal candidate in that county in the last election and a very respectable gentleman, Mr. Caldwell, and the other being a clergyman. They made a report in which they stated, under their own signature, that this mother was certainly entitled to receive the money for the children instead of the corner grocer. Notwithstanding that, the commission decidted that the money must still be paid to this outside party. The principle involved in a case of this kind is a very important one. It is only in a most exceptional case that the parent should be deprived of handling pension money, and the evidence ought to be absolutely irrefutable. Just, upon this point, I want to say that, in my judgment and having some knowledge of the work of this commission since its inception, it has not performed its work in as satisfactory a manner as I should like to have seen it do. The chairman of the commission, a very respectable gentleman, was too busy to give his time to the matter, and I know, to my personal knowledge, that during the past year one commissioner alone was sitting and dealing with these cases. It has only been within the last few months, since Major Coristine was promoted from the office of secretary to a commissioner, that the work has been carried on in any reasonably businesslike manner. Numerous complaints have come to me from

soldiers and their families about the delays and dilly-dallying and unsatisfactory manner in which their complaints are heard, and about their reference from one person to another until they have travelled several miles in order to find out just where they must lodge their complaints to have them attended to. I trust the Government, who have now the chairmanship to fill, will see to it that a man who is accustomed to dealing with business matters and who also has some heartr-because this Act ought to be interpreted liberally in favour of those whom we wish to benefit-is appointed to that position. In my judgment-and I say it with a good deal of regret-that the commission has not been managed in a businesslike way and in the interest of those to-whom the Parliament of 'Canada intended that the benefit should go under the provisions of the Act. The case I have mentioned is a case in point. But the commission did more than that. I applied to the Militia Department in this case, and they refused to give this man the handling of this money; they gave the woman an allowance because her son overseas was her sole support, the father being an imbecile. The Board of Pension Commissioners in this case said: We will deprive you of the $16 for the children; you must take either the one allowance or the other. When the Militia Department granted $20 a month to this poor worn air who had lost two sons and had two younger children at home to support, the Pension Board absolutely refused to pay the $16 any longer, even through this third party. These are circumstances which have come to my notice. I submit that subclause (3) ought to be amended and that in no case ought the pension to be paid to an outside person as long as there is a mother or a father or a legal guardian to receive it. We have no right to sit in judgment upon the moral conduct of the mother or father who has given two sons to carry on this war, and the sons, as a result of their services, have died. Judging by the experience that I have had in the case I have mentioned, it is not satisfactory to leave this in the hands of the Board of Pension Commissioners who, as the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) has very well said,- and I adopt his remarks-must and do rely upon the report of their inspector who casually goes about and looks into the home of a soldier's wife and says: I do not think she is clean, or tidy, or something of that kind, and reports against her case. That is not right and I should like to see the words- " or to a person appointed by the commission "-struck out of this subclause and
limited to cases where there is no mother nor father nor legal guardian.

While on general principles there may be a great deal to be said for what the hon. member (Mr. Fripp) has just told the House, I think, if he will consider the matter oarefully, he will reach the conclusion that there are many cases where there is a mother living, yet where it would be improper that the pension money in respect of the children should be paid to her. The prime object the commission must always consider is this:	Is the
money being wisely spent by the person to whom it is being paid in order to advance the interest of the child or children, as the case may be? I would readily concur in what my hon. friend says that "To err is human," but although the commission may have made a mistake in some isolated case-I cannot say whether or not they have made a mistake in the case in which he has directed our attention,-yet the Committee will see how unwise it would be to make the Act declare that, if there is a mother, no matter what her conduct or character may be, or no matter whether she is spending the money for the benefit of the children or no't, the money must be paid to her. The first object of the commission must surely be to see that the interests of the children are being protected, and I think that is the object of this section as drafted. My hon. friend is quite correct in stating that the commission has limped a bit this year, owing to the fact that one member died, another member then resigned and a third, a short time later, handed in his resignation. I understand 'it is hoped soon to complete the commission, and I am sure the Government hope that no further mistakes such as those to which our attention has been directed will occur.
Why not have a guardian appointed by the court as in ordinary cases?
If the mother is not a fit subject to receive the money to be expended on behalf of the children, it is very easy to appoint a guardian.

If the case my hon. friend has cited is true, I do not think this is an error, it is a crime. Such cases ought not to happen. Instead of having the appointment made by the commission why not have it made by the court?
Mr. LEMtIEUX: The court will consider the friends of the familv
>
There is a procedure established and very properly so, and I think that would be the better protection for the children, if the mother were not a fit subject to handle money.

Why not place this under the care of the Children's Aid Society which is an efficient organization and is to be found in every community of any size or account in this country? It would handle cases of this kind very efficiently. -
The practice has been, where there is a Children's Aid Society, to take advantage of its services. I understand that there are no such societies in Quebec.

We have many other
societies.

Advantage is taken of any machinery that is available, and, I understand, advantage is taken of every charitable or other organization that will assist. The appointment of a guardian means expense, sometimes substantial expense. A woman might be laid up in hospital for a month or two, and it might not be wise to go to the expense of appointing a guardian just while the mother was ill.

That would be an isolated case; it would be an accident. We are not legislating for isolated cases, but for the mass of people concerned. If the mother is sick in the hospital, we do not want to see the children on the street. Why not let the actual guardian in whose care the children are handle the money for the month or two months the mother is in the hospital?

The section is drawn for exactly that purpose. My hon. friend has taken the language out of my mouth, except that he has expressed himself better than I could. "The pension for a johild shall be paid to its mother or father, or to its guardian, or to a person appointed by the commission." If the mother had named some suitable person to discharge her duty during her absence at the hospital the commission would pay the money to her. The object is simply to see that the children are protected-and as cheaply as possible.

From the case cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp) it would seem the board acted in a very arbitrary manner when they chose to pay the money to a corner grocer instead of to the woman, although Air. Caldwell, who is well known 
to members of this House, and a clergyman had reported in her favour. There is something wrong with the commission when it acts in that way, if the facts are as reported, and I am sure they are, because my hon. friend (Air. Fripp) says so.

If the facts are as represented by the hon. member (Mr. Fripp), and I am satisfied that as far as he knows them they are, it would appear that the money should have been paid over to the mother. The committee will understand that it is impossible for the minister and myself to know the facts in an isolated case of which we had no notice prior to the .hon. member (Mr. Fripp) rising a few moments ago.

It shows the necessity of guarding against the board acting upon the report of some visitor into the home.
I submit that the person who should make the inquiry is the county judge, and that would give the mother or the father a chance to be heard before they were deprived of the pension money. In this particular case the parent was deprived of the pension upon the report of an officer of the commission, without giving the other side of the case a chance to be heard at all. Neither the mother nor the father was called before the commission to answer the report of the visitor; they were deprived of the pension in their absence. I submit that the committee should guard against anything like that happening in the future by providing that the county judge or some other official shall hear both sides before depriving the parent of what I submit is his clear right to receive a pension in respect of a member of his family who has been killed.

I submit that the suggestion I have made would work admirably in the province of Ontario at all events. I have a case in mind in the town of Renfrew where the funds are being disbursed from month 'to month by the president of the Children's Aid Society. That has been going on for some time, and there lias been no friction. Why should the county judge be named to deal with a case of that kind? I question whether he would give as efficient service as the president of the Children's Aid Society in isolated cases of that kind. I submit that the Children's Aid Society can handle these cases more efficiently and more economically.

I think it would meet the view of the hon. member (Mr. Bureau) and the hon. member (Mr. Fripp) if the subsection read this way:
The pension for a child shall he paid to its father, mother or guardian or to a person appointed by a Court of Record.
That would cover both Ontario and the other provinces. It would only confuse matters to introduce the Children's Aid Society, because in some provinces that society does not exist, and where it does exist, in many cases it is not well operated.
We could say "or to the person before whom the applications for guardian are made."

I think the subsection is better as it is. It will only lead to more trouble if you allow applications to the courts. If the commission is properly constituted it will get along all right. If not, there will be trouble from here to Halifax.

I certainly endorse the
clause as it stands. I think it is the cheapest way to administer the Act. The board afe not prejudiced against any person. Why should we not leave it to their judgment to say whether a person is fit to have the money paid over to him? It has to be left to the judgment of somebody, and the board and their inspectors have just as good judgment as ony one else who might be specified.
The board have no interest in not doing what is absolutely right; their only object is to see that the money of the country is properly expended, and that is the object of this clause. This matter was discussed at great length in the Pensions Committee, and eventually we made up our minds that this was the better way to do it, and I believe so still.

I have every respect for the conclusions of the Pensions Committee, but the case cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp) appeals to me. In that case the commission acted upon the report of an inspector, and you would require a perfect inspector to decide these cases, and such a one cannot be found in spite of all the aspirations and work done by certain gentlemen for higher morals. It all depends
upon the mood the inspector is in, upon how he feels when he gets up in the morning, which depends upon what he did the night before. That man is human. I say that we should, use the judicial organizations already existing. The prothonotary in Quebec, who appoints the guardians, knows exactly how to go about it, and the expense would be nothing. We have such a thing as pleading in forma pauperis. I am satisfied that as far as the province of Quebec is concerned the judicial expenses that would be incurred would be remitted. I will support the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) if he puts it as an amendment. I think that the subsection ought to be amended to protect the children dependent upon the soldier. It is extraordinary that the commission should, as in the case mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp), act upon the report of one of their inspectors, without giving the interested parties a chance to present their case, and we should provide against anything of that kind happening in the future.
I do not know anything about the case my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp) has cited. He did not state that he had looked into the case personally.
Yes, I did.

I know that the Committee looked into dozens of cases that were cited to us, and invariably we found that they were not correctly reported to us in the first place, and that the Pension Commissioners were right.

The Board of Pension Commissioners, from my personal knowledge, did not investigate any of these oases, and the gentleman who is present and who works in the office knows that they are done in a perfunctory way by clerks, and that the pension commissioners are absent, and have been during the past year. For months there has not been one on duty attending to his work in Ottawa. There is no use talking about the pension commissioners giving personal attention to these matters; they do not do anything of the kind. These reports are passed upon at once and accepted, and the public, those who are entitled to receive pensions, receive poor treatment. It is our duty to protect these children and others entitled to pensions, and there should be no superficial administration such as I have mentioned, and which I know goes on in this and other departments.
Goes on now?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: , As the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) said, we had before us a great many complaints with reference to the work of the Pensions Board. A number of statements were made before the committee similar to the statements made by the hon. member for Ottawa. We bad all those cases looked into and I must say in justice to the Pensions Board and its administration that the complaints, as the hon. member for Kingston mentioned, were not found to be justified. In the great majority of cases, with very few exceptions, we found that they were administering the law as it stood, and the real ground of complaint was that they were not in a position . to grant pension or allowance in the particular case complained of because the regulations did not permit of its being granted.
That is a different case.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know. I am only speaking of general complaints. Of course, I know nothing about the case mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa. But take these clauses dealing with children, and matters of a kindred character. The committee had before them officers of the Pensions Board. We examined them at length and got all the information we could, and finally reached the conclusion that these clauses were wise. It was deemed wise to give certain discretion to 'the commission, particularly in dealing with children who are entitled to receive pension where there is no one to properly care for them and see that they are maintained out of the pension. With regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) with reference to the appointment of a guardian by a court of record, there is expense incidental to this matter. If you cannot pay the pension over without a guardian being appointed and without the incidental delay, it will mean the cost of appointing the guardian, and other expense in connection with the guardianship. We must give some discretion to the board and trust it somewhat, and that was the view of the ccommittee. With reference to the general work of the board, I do not think it is fair to compare the present situation with the regrettable condition that developed last summer and to which my hon. friend has already alluded. One of the members of the board who was always here and always in attendance, resigned. Later, the two other members of the board resigned, largely because of the resolution of the com-
mittee of a year ago which demanded that they should give their whole time to the work and that every pension awarded should be evidenced by the signature of at least one commissioner. There are now two pension commissioners here on the work all the time, both returned soldiers who have no interests to serve other than those of the Pension Board. The new Bill requires that the commissioners shall not be engaged in any other occupation inconsistent with their work, to which they must devote their whole time, and we have every reason to anticipate that the Board of Pensions Commissioners from now on will be composed of three men devoting their whole time to the duties in connection with the office. I feel sure that the committee of this House, a large and representative committee, reached a wise conclusion when they settled this very difficult section in the form in which it was decided on, and I am only voicing what was the judgment of the committee in supporting their recommendation made after careful consideration.
The argument of my hon. friend does not exactly answer the statement of the hon. member for Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know nothing of the facts. There may have been an executive blunder, but it does not appear to me that we should frame the law to meet a particular case because a mistake may Have been made and one that is incidental to administration and may have grown out of the condition of one commissioner having resigned, and there having been a transition period in the management of the board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does not the minister think that it is a fair time to wind' up now?
I was hoping that we would pass the section and then be half through the Bill.
The statement is made that complaints were made to the board and in most cases they proved futile.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In most cases they proved not to be cases of maladministration or of lack of consideration, but of failure to decide in accordance with what the applicant thought was right, this being due to the regulations-the law which this House had recommended and which was in force.
' Sir HERBERT AMES: I can corroborate that from cases which occur daily. The Patriotic Fund are constantly being asked to investigate pension cases for people who feel that they do not get what they deserve, and almost invariably we find that, it is not

the fault of the Pension Commissioners, but of the regulations under which they are operating. They are asked to do something which the applicant thinks they should do and which could not be done under the regulations as they formerly stood. Three-quarters of the claims we found, on thorough investigation, to be not ^ell founded.

This is different entirely. When a man claims that he is entitled to a pension it is one thing; but when he is entitled to it and it is not properly paid, that is a different thing. If I understand the President of the Privy Council rightly, he said that these cases were investigated. He said: "We had the commissioners before us." Well, surely the commissioners would not be men if they did not make the best of their case.
We had the complainants too.
I would take 'the word of my hon. friend, the member for Ottawa, as against the judgment of the commissioner every time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 3 carry?
There ,is a motion by the hon. member for North Perth.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: AH motions should be presented in writing.
I withdraw the motion.

I think that in trying to avoid what the hon. member for Ottawa points out, we are going to pass legislation that will make possible a great many hardships which he has no thought of putting into the Act. This money is for the benefit of the child, and we want to make it possible for it to reach the child and no one else. We want to take the most sympathetic method, and I do not think that there is any one who understands the situation better than the Pension Commissioners. If you are going to hedge that all around by legal processes and make it necessary to have a court procedure every time money is to be paid to some one else than the parent you will occasion delay.
You will have difficulties and disputes in the meantime and, farther than that, you will have cases perhaps for one or two months when the money should be paid to some one else and then should go back to the father and mother again. You will have to appoint guardians and unappoint them a week afterwards, and there will be a great deal of trouble and legal technicality
None whatever.

The simplest
method possible would be the best for the child. We have had a good deal to do with the pension commissioners and I must confess that we have found them, while not invariably right-nine times out of ten right. They reach the result in a simple, sympathetic and prompt manner which you will not do if you put this into a court of law.
I fail to see the sympathy in the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Ottawa.

I would like to say a
word in support of the contention of the hon. gentleman (Sir Herbert Ames) and to cite a case where the arrangement that he speaks of has worked out to advantage. A member of the Canadian army who joined in Calgary was married to a young woman from a village in my constituency. When he went to the front, she left Calgary and came home to that village. She brought her mother and two small children with her. The man was killed in the war and a pension was obtained for the wife. Shortly after, the wife died also leaving these children to her mother, and the pension was transferred to the mother. In August of last summer the grandmother died and the children reverted to an aunt. The circumstances of these people were not very good. An effort was made to have the pension transferred to the children, but through some hitch for about four months the children did not get the pension. Christmas was coming on, with cold weather, and they were not supplied with their winter clothing. Fortunately, the aunt met me on the train and she brought this matter to my attention. I took it up with the board in Ottawa, got an immediate reference to Toronto, and inside of two days the cheque was there for the children to provide them with clothing and things for Christmas. There must be a direct, quick method of dealing with these cases.
Every one is not fortunate enough every day to meet an hon. gentleman with the influence of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie).

Members of this House
will always be willing to act in cases of this kind, and they should be allowed to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved in amendment that paragraph 3 of section 23 be amended by striking out the words " the

commission " in the 14th and 15th lines, page 8, and substituting therefor the words " a court of record."
Amendment negatived.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 24-orphan child:
I would like to get a definition of "unmarried wife."

Before adopting this
phraseology with respect to this domestic relationship the following definition of unmarried wife was arrived at:
A woman who, although not married to the member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he became a member of the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who, at such time, was publicly represented by him as his wife, shall for the purposes of this Act, be considered to have been his unmarried wife.
I think that gives a clear definition of what is meant by the term.
What are you reading from?
Subsection 3 of section 33.
Surely there is no such thing as an "unmarried wife"?

This is the definition
given.

There are very many countries where at common law a woman living with a man and acknowledged by him as his wife, becomes his wife. That is Scotch law. In Scotland, in New York state and in California, this primary law is well recognized. I would suggest that tl;e better term to use would be "his common law wife."
Section agreed to7 on division.
Progress reported.

Saturday, June 28, 1919.
